orig_9709_s1_bg_binomial_models.description: Justify the binomial model, count success positions, and calculate exact, tail and interval probabilities with the correct integer endpoints.

sections.title: What is one trial, and what counts as a success?
sections.label: Model assumptions
sections.intro:
A binomial random variable counts successes in a fixed number of trials. Before writing a formula, identify the physical trial and the event called success. Then check the model assumptions:

  • The number of trials \(n\) is fixed in advance.
  • Each trial is classified as success or failure for the chosen count.
  • The success indicators from different trials are independent.
  • The success probability \(p\) is the same on every trial.

Under these conditions, write

\[X\sim\mathrm{B}(n,p).\]

The first parameter is the trial count; the second is the probability of the success that \(X\) counts. They have different meanings and are not interchangeable.

blocks.title: Stop and think: which procedure matches the binomial trial model?
blocks.prompt: A bag contains two gold and three silver tokens. Which procedure directly satisfies the standard fixed-trial binomial assumptions using the per-draw gold probability \(\frac{2}{5}\)? For that procedure, state \(n\) and \(p\).

options.replace: Make four independent uniform draws, returning and mixing the token after every draw.
options.remove: Make four uniform draws without returning any token.
options.stop: Draw with replacement and stop as soon as the first gold token appears.

fields.label: Number of trials in the binomial procedure
Success probability in the binomial procedure

blocks.hint: A binomial count needs a fixed number of trials, independent success indicators and the same success probability throughout.
blocks.solution: 1. The first procedure has four fixed independent trials, each with gold probability \(\frac{2}{5}\), so its gold count is \(\mathrm{B}(4,\frac{2}{5})\). Without replacement the success indicators are dependent. Stopping at the first gold does not use a fixed number of trials.

blocks.html: Define success in terms of the requested variable. A defect, a failure of equipment or a score below a threshold can all be called success in a binomial model. Once the definition is fixed, use its probability \(p\) and the complementary failure probability \(1-p\) consistently.

The possible listed counts are \(0,1,\ldots,n\). For \(0<p<1\), every one has positive probability. At \(p=0\), the count is always zero; at \(p=1\), it is always \(n\). Handle these constant cases directly, without relying on an ambiguous expression such as \(0^0\).

sections.title: Why does the count event need a combination factor?
sections.label: Patterns and orders
sections.intro:
For one specified success/failure string containing \(r\) successes and \(n-r\) failures, independence gives probability

\[p^r(1-p)^{n-r}.\]

The count event “exactly \(r\) successes” usually allows many strings. Choose which \(r\) of the \(n\) labelled trial positions contain successes:

\[\binom{n}{r}=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}.\]

Each permitted position set gives one string. These strings are disjoint and have the same probability because they have the same numbers of success and failure factors.

blocks.html:
Exactly two successes in five trials

In each independent trial, \(P(\mathrm{S})=\frac{2}{5}\) and \(P(\mathrm{F})=\frac{3}{5}\). Choose the two successful positions in \(\binom{5}{2}=10\) ways.

Success positionsTrial sequence
1 and 2S S F F F
1 and 3S F S F F
1 and 4S F F S F
1 and 5S F F F S
2 and 3F S S F F
2 and 4F S F S F
2 and 5F S F F S
3 and 4F F S S F
3 and 5F F S F S
4 and 5F F F S S

One specified pattern has probability \(\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^2\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^3=\frac{108}{3125}\).

The patterns are disjoint and equally likely, so \(P(X=2)=10\times\frac{108}{3125}=\frac{216}{625}\).

The ten choices of two success positions give ten disjoint strings with the same probability. The probability of the unrestricted count event is their sum.

blocks.title: Separate a specified pattern from an unrestricted count
blocks.prompt: Four independent trials have success probability \(\frac{1}{3}\). Find the probability of the specified pattern SFFF, the number of distinct patterns with exactly one success, and the probability of exactly one success in any order.
blocks.hint: The specified pattern has one success factor and three failure factors. For any order, choose which one of the four trial positions contains the success.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(\mathrm{SFFF})=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^3=\frac{8}{81}.\]
  2. \[\binom{4}{1}=4,\qquad P(X=1)=4\cdot\frac{8}{81}=\frac{32}{81}.\]

blocks.html: Do not add the combination factor to a specified order. If the question already fixes every success and failure position, its probability is one product. Use \(\binom{n}{r}\) when the success positions may be any of the \(r\)-element subsets of the \(n\) trials.

The coefficient is one when \(r=0\) or \(r=n\): there is one all-failure string and one all-success string. It is not an additional probability, so it may exceed one; the complete weighted expression must still lie between zero and one.

sections.title: How is an exact count probability calculated?
sections.label: Exact probabilities
sections.intro:
Combining the equal-weight pattern calculation with the number of success-position sets gives the binomial probability formula:

\[P(X=r)=\binom{n}{r}p^r(1-p)^{n-r},\qquad r=0,1,\ldots,n.\]

Read the expression as a position count multiplied by a success factor and a failure factor. The two exponents add to \(n\), the total trial count. An impossible count, such as a negative count, a count above \(n\), or a noninteger count, has probability zero.

blocks.title: Check the success exponent and the remaining failure count
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(5,\frac{1}{4})\). Find the exact probabilities \(P(X=2)\) and \(P(X=0)\).
blocks.hint: Two successes leave three failures. No successes means all five trials fail, and there is only one such success/failure pattern.

blocks.html: Record the distribution and the requested event before using a calculator. A probability-mass operation calculates one exact count. A cumulative operation usually totals counts up to and including its upper bound. Check the convention instead of treating these operations as interchangeable.

Keep exact fractions or unrounded calculator values through a multi-term calculation, and round only the final probability to the requested precision. For a percentage, multiply the final probability by one hundred and label it as a percentage.

sections.title: Which integer counts are included by the wording?
sections.label: Tails and intervals
sections.intro:
Translate the words into an event before evaluating it. For an integer threshold \(k\),

WordingEventIncluded counts or complement
Exactly \(k\)\(X=k\)One count
At most \(k\)\(X\le k\)Counts up to and including \(k\)
Fewer than \(k\)\(X<k\)\(X\le k-1\)
At least \(k\)\(X\ge k\)\(1-P(X\le k-1)\)
More than \(k\)\(X>k\)\(1-P(X\le k)\)

Intersect the event with the actual count range \(0,1,\ldots,n\). For a noninteger threshold, list the permitted integer counts directly; the one-step endpoint shifts above are stated for integer \(k\).

blocks.title: At least one and more than one exclude different lower tails
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(4,\frac{1}{3})\). Find \(P(X\ge1)\) and \(P(X>1)\).

fields.label: Probability of at least one success
Probability of more than one success

blocks.hint: For at least one, exclude only zero. For more than one, exclude both zero and one.

blocks.html:
The highlighted counts are \(2,3,4\). Their total is \(P(1<X<5)=\frac{15+20+15}{64}=\frac{25}{32}\).

For more than one but fewer than five successes, the included bars are exactly two, three and four. The excluded tails each have total probability seven sixty-fourths.

blocks.title: List the integer values before evaluating an interval
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(5,\frac{1}{2})\). For “at least two but fewer than four”, give the smallest and largest included counts and the probability. Then find the probability of “more than two but at most four”.

fields.label: Smallest count in the first event
Largest count in the first event

blocks.hint: The first event includes two and three. The second includes three and four. Each specified five-trial pattern has probability \(\frac{1}{32}\).

blocks.html:
If \(F(k)=P(X\le k)\), an inclusive integer interval satisfies

\[P(a\le X\le b)=F(b)-F(a-1).\]

The subtraction removes every count below \(a\) while leaving \(a\) itself included. If the event is \(a<X\le b\), subtract \(F(a)\) instead. A quick list of included integers is often the safest way to choose the bounds.

The complement must be the exact opposite event. The opposite of at least \(k\) is fewer than \(k\), not at most \(k\). When subtracting two tails for an interval, check that they are disjoint and that neither includes a desired boundary value.

sections.title: Do the physical assumptions justify an exact binomial model?
sections.label: Model checks
sections.intro: A fixed trial count and two success categories do not by themselves establish a binomial model. Check independence and the constant success probability using the experiment’s actual structure. A changing population, a shared hidden state, copied outcomes or different success probabilities can invalidate the standard formula.

blocks.title: Constant marginal probability does not establish independence
blocks.prompt: A fair coin is tossed once. Its result is then copied into six labelled record positions. Let \(X\) count the positions labelled heads. Every individual position has head probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). Is \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(6,\frac{1}{2})\)? Find the actual probabilities \(P(X=3)\) and \(P(X=6)\).

options.dependent: The binomial model is invalid because the six recorded indicators are dependent.
options.binomial: The model is binomial because there are six records and each has head probability one half.
options.equal: Every count from zero to six is equally likely.

fields.label: Actual probability of three recorded heads
Actual probability of six recorded heads

blocks.hint: There is only one coin toss. Either all six records are heads or all six are tails.
blocks.solution: 1. The actual distribution has \(P(X=0)=\frac{1}{2}\), \(P(X=6)=\frac{1}{2}\), and zero probability at all intermediate counts. Hence \(P(X=3)=0\). The success indicators are completely linked, so their equal marginal probabilities cannot justify binomial multiplication.

blocks.html: Separate marginal probabilities from conditional probabilities. In a fixed-composition sample without replacement, each labelled draw position can have the same marginal red probability while the draws remain dependent. Multiplication of unconditional success probabilities requires independence.

Sampling a very small fraction of a sufficiently large population without replacement can sometimes be modelled approximately as binomial because the composition changes little. State that this is an approximation and explain why it is reasonable in the given context; do not describe a small-population calculation as exact binomial sampling.

Likewise, independent trials with different success probabilities do not generally have the standard binomial count distribution. Stopping as soon as a success occurs changes the trial count from fixed to random. Recheck the model whenever the procedure changes.

Explain the relevant assumption in context. “The draws are without replacement, so the next success probability depends on earlier colours” is a model explanation. Merely listing the four binomial conditions without relating them to the experiment does not show whether they hold.

glossary.definition: A success count from a fixed number of independent trials with constant success probability.
One repetition of the experiment whose outcome is classified as success or failure.
Whether a particular trial satisfies the event being counted.
The constant probability p of the event counted as a success on one trial.
The labelled trial positions in which successes occur.
The probability that the count equals one specified integer value.
The probability that a count is at most a specified upper value.
An event that includes counts on one side of a threshold.
A bound that excludes its endpoint, using less than or greater than.
A condition about the experiment that justifies using a probability distribution.

examples.title: Define one trial and the success being counted
examples.question: A fair die with faces numbered one to six is rolled independently eight times. Let \(X\) count the rolls on which the score is at least four. State a suitable distribution for \(X\), explaining every parameter and model assumption.
solution: One trial is one die roll. Call a score of four, five or six a success; the other three faces are failures for this particular count. Each roll therefore contributes either one success or none.

The number of trials is fixed at \(n=8\). The rolls are independent, and the die stays fair on every roll. Hence the success probability stays constant:

\[p=P(\text{score at least }4)=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}.\]

Therefore

\[X\sim\mathrm{B}\left(8,\frac{1}{2}\right),\qquad X\in\{0,1,\ldots,8\}.\]

The die has six physical outcomes, but only two success categories for this variable. The binomial condition concerns the success indicator for each trial; it does not require the underlying experiment to have only two physical outcomes.

examples.title: One specified pattern is not the whole count event
examples.question: Five independent trials each have success probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). Find the probability of the specified pattern SSFFF, then the probability of exactly two successes in any order.
solution:
For SSFFF, the two success positions and three failure positions are fixed. Independence gives

\[P(\mathrm{SSFFF})=\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^2\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^3=\frac{108}{3125}.\]

Exactly two successes may occupy any two of the five positions. The number of position sets is

\[\binom{5}{2}=\frac{5!}{2!3!}=10.\]

Every such pattern has two factors \(\frac{2}{5}\) and three factors \(\frac{3}{5}\), so its probability is the same as the specified pattern. These ten patterns are disjoint:

\[P(X=2)=10\cdot\frac{108}{3125}=\frac{216}{625}.\]

The combination factor counts the positions of the successes. It does not reorder labelled physical trials or assume that every possible success/failure string has equal probability. Strings with different numbers of successes generally have different weights when \(p\ne\frac{1}{2}\).

examples.title: Substitute the counted success probability into the exact formula
examples.question: There are eight questions, each with four answer options and exactly one correct option. A student chooses uniformly and independently among the options on each question. Let \(X\) be the number correct. Find \(P(X=3)\), giving an exact value and a decimal to three significant figures.
solution: A success is a correct answer. Thus \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(8,\frac{1}{4})\), and the failure probability is \(\frac{3}{4}\).

Exactly three successes leave five failures:

\[P(X=3)=\binom{8}{3}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^3\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^5.\]
To three significant figures, the required probability is \(0.208\). Keep the unrounded value during the calculation; a binomial probability is a number between zero and one, not a count of answers.

examples.title: Use the complement for at least one success
examples.question: Twelve components are tested independently. Each has probability \(\frac{1}{10}\) of being defective, with the same probability for every component. Find the probability that at least one component is defective, to three significant figures.
solution:
Define a success as finding a defective component. For the number of defectives,

\[X\sim\mathrm{B}\left(12,\frac{1}{10}\right).\]

The word “success” is a model label; the event need not be desirable.

The complement of at least one defective is no defectives:

\[P(X\ge1)=1-P(X=0).\]

All twelve must be nondefective for \(X=0\), giving

\[P(X\ge1)=1-\left(\frac{9}{10}\right)^{12}=0.717570463519.\]
The answer is \(0.718\) to three significant figures. This avoids adding twelve separate binomial terms and keeps the rounding to the final step.

examples.title: At most and fewer than have different endpoints
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(6,\frac{1}{3})\). Find the probabilities of at most two successes and of fewer than two successes.
solution: At most two includes zero, one and two. Fewer than two includes only zero and one because \(X\) is an integer.

The required individual terms are

\[P(X=0)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^6=\frac{64}{729},\]\[P(X=1)=\binom{6}{1}\cdot\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^5=\frac{192}{729},\]\[P(X=2)=\binom{6}{2}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^4=\frac{240}{729}.\]
The difference is exactly \(P(X=2)=\frac{240}{729}\), the boundary value included by “at most” but excluded by “fewer than”.

examples.title: Translate a strict interval before using sums or cumulative values
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(6,\frac{1}{2})\). Find the probability of more than one but fewer than five successes. Show a direct sum and a complementary or cumulative method.
solution:
The phrase means \(1<X<5\). The included integer counts are two, three and four:

\[P(1<X<5)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)+P(X=4).\]

All six-trial strings have probability \(\frac{1}{64}\) because the success probability is \(\frac{1}{2}\). Thus

\[P(1<X<5)=\frac{\binom{6}{2}+\binom{6}{3}+\binom{6}{4}}{64}=\frac{15+20+15}{64}=\frac{25}{32}.\]

The excluded lower counts are zero and one, with total probability \(\frac{7}{64}\). The excluded upper counts are five and six, also with total \(\frac{7}{64}\):

\[P(1<X<5)=1-\frac{7}{64}-\frac{7}{64}=\frac{25}{32}.\]

If \(F(k)=P(X\le k)\), the same event is

\[P(2\le X\le4)=F(4)-F(1)=\frac{57}{64}-\frac{7}{64}=\frac{25}{32}.\]

Subtract the cumulative probability through one, not through two, because the value two must remain included.

examples.title: A small sample without replacement needs a different exact model
examples.question: A bag contains eight distinct balls: three red and five blue. Three are selected uniformly without replacement. Let \(X\) be the red count. Explain why \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(3,\frac{3}{8})\) is not the exact model, and find the exact probability of one red.
solution: The number of draws is fixed and each draw can be classified red or blue. However, the colour of an earlier draw changes the remaining composition. After a first red, the next red probability is \(\frac{2}{7}\); after a first blue, it is \(\frac{3}{7}\). The success indicators are dependent.

The first-draw red probability \(\frac{3}{8}\) cannot be multiplied repeatedly as if the draws were independent. The marginal red probability at each fixed draw position is still \(\frac{3}{8}\); that fact alone does not establish independence.

There are \(\binom{8}{3}=56\) equally likely three-ball subsets. For one red, choose one of the three reds and two of the five blues:

\[P(X=1)=\frac{\binom{3}{1}\binom{5}{2}}{\binom{8}{3}}=\frac{30}{56}=\frac{15}{28}.\]

The binomial calculation would instead give

\[\binom{3}{1}\cdot\frac{3}{8}\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)^2=\frac{225}{512},\]

which differs from the exact probability. In this small finite population, replacement and independence cannot be assumed.

extraPractice.title: Check the experiment rather than the word success
extraPractice.prompt:
Decide whether an exact binomial model describes each stated count.

A: Five counters are drawn without replacement from a bag containing three red and seven blue counters; count the reds.

B: Six independent tests are made, each positive with probability \(0.3\); count the positive tests.

C: A fair coin is tossed until its first head; count the number of tosses made.

D: Ten independent trials are performed; success probability is \(0.2\) on each of the first five and \(0.5\) on each of the last five; count all successes.

options.no: No: the stated count is not binomial

extraPractice.hint: Check a fixed number of trials, a success/failure classification, independence and the same success probability on every trial. The variable must count successes in those trials.
extraPractice.solution:
1. A: no. Without replacement, the available colour counts change with earlier draws. The trials are not independent with a constant red probability; an exact finite-sampling model is required.

  2. B: yes. There are six fixed independent trials, each with the same positive probability \(0.3\). For the count \(X\),

    \[X\sim\mathrm{B}(6,0.3).\]

  3. C: no. The number of trials is not fixed in advance, and the variable counts the waiting time to a first head rather than heads in a fixed trial total.

  4. D: no. Independence and a fixed number of trials are present, but the success probability is not constant across all ten trials. Averaging the two probabilities does not make this count exactly binomial.

extraPractice.title: A specified order has no combination factor
extraPractice.prompt: A player makes seven independent shots, each successful with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). Write S for a success and F for a failure. Find the probability of the particular ordered sequence SSFFSFF, the number of different success/failure sequences containing exactly three successes, and the probability of exactly three successes in any order.
extraPractice.hint: The specified sequence has three successes and four failures. To obtain any order, choose which three of the seven positions contain the successes. Every such sequence has the same probability.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(SSFFSFF)=\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^3\cdot\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^4=\frac{648}{78125}.\]

    This is one already specified order, so no extra position factor belongs here.

  2. \[N_{\text{orders}}=\binom{7}{3}=35.\]

    Choosing the success positions also determines all four failure positions.

  3. \[P(X=3)=\binom{7}{3}\cdot\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^3\cdot\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^4=35\cdot\frac{648}{78125}=\frac{4536}{15625}.\]

    Do not multiply by another factorial to order identical S and F symbols.

extraPractice.title: Exact probabilities include the support endpoints
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}\left(9,\frac{1}{3}\right)\). Find \(P(X=0)\) and \(P(X=2)\), each to four decimal places. Give the exact value of \(P(X=10)\).
extraPractice.hint: The success probability is \(\frac{1}{3}\), so failure probability is \(\frac{2}{3}\). In nine trials the count can only be an integer from zero to nine.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(X=0)=\binom{9}{0}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^0\cdot\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^9=\frac{512}{19683}\approx0.0260\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]
  2. \[P(X=2)=\binom{9}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\cdot\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^7=\frac{512}{2187}\approx0.2341\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

  3. Ten successes cannot occur in nine trials. Therefore \(P(X=10)=0\); do not substitute an impossible count into a factorial expression.

extraPractice.title: Translate each endpoint before choosing a calculation
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(10,0.2)\). Find \(P(X\ge1)\), \(P(X>2)\), \(P(2\le X\le4)\) and \(P(X<2)\). Give every probability to four decimal places.
extraPractice.hint: For an integer count, above two means at least three and below two means at most one. An inclusive interval retains both its endpoints. Complements often require fewer terms.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(X\ge1)=1-P(X=0)=1-0.8^{10}\approx0.8926\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]
  2. \[P(X>2)=1-\sum_{r=0}^{2}\binom{10}{r}\cdot0.2^r\cdot0.8^{10-r}\approx0.3222\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

    Subtracting only the probabilities at zero and one would incorrectly include the value two.

  3. \[P(2\le X\le4)=\sum_{r=2}^{4}\binom{10}{r}\cdot0.2^r\cdot0.8^{10-r}\approx0.5914\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]
  4. \[P(X<2)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)=0.8^{10}+10\cdot0.2\cdot0.8^9\approx0.3758\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

    Keep unrounded terms until the complete event probability is calculated.

extraPractice.title: Two or more failures is the complement of zero or one
extraPractice.prompt: Twelve sensors operate independently. Each has probability \(0.08\) of failing a test. Let \(F\) be the number that fail. Find the probability that none fails, that at most one fails, and that at least two fail. Give each answer to four decimal places.
extraPractice.hint: Use failure as the counted success, so \(F\sim\mathrm{B}(12,0.08)\). At least two failures is the complement of both zero and one failure, not just the complement of zero.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(F=0)=0.92^{12}\approx0.3677\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]
  2. \[P(F\le1)=0.92^{12}+\binom{12}{1}\cdot0.08\cdot0.92^{11}\approx0.7513\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]
  3. \[P(F\ge2)=1-P(F\le1)\approx0.2487\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

    The two final events partition the full sample space. This provides a useful check that their probabilities sum to one before rounding.

starters.title: Choose the counted outcome and translate the pass count
starters.question: Fifteen devices are tested independently. Each passes with probability \(0.9\). Let \(F\) be the number that fail. State the two parameters \(n\) and \(p\) in the binomial model for \(F\). Then find the probability of exactly two failures, the probability of no more than two failures, and the probability that between eleven and thirteen devices inclusive pass. Give the three event probabilities to four decimal places.
starters.hint: The variable counts failures, so its binomial probability is \(0.1\). The number of passes is \(15-F\); translate both endpoints of the pass interval into failure counts.
starters.solution:
1. There are fifteen fixed trials, each with independent failure probability \(0.1\). Thus

    \[F\sim\mathrm{B}(15,0.1),\qquad n=15,\quad p=\frac{1}{10}.\]
  2. \[P(F=2)=\binom{15}{2}\cdot0.1^2\cdot0.9^{13}\approx0.2669\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]
  3. \[P(F\le2)=\sum_{r=0}^{2}\binom{15}{r}\cdot0.1^r\cdot0.9^{15-r}\approx0.8159\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

  4. The pass condition is \(11\le15-F\le13\), which is equivalent to \(2\le F\le4\). Therefore

    \[P(11\le\text{passes}\le13)=\sum_{r=2}^{4}\binom{15}{r}\cdot0.1^r\cdot0.9^{15-r}\approx0.4382\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

    The lower pass endpoint becomes the upper failure endpoint, so check both bounds after reversing the count.

starters.title: Wins and losses describe the same fixed experiment
starters.question: A player completes ten independent rounds. In each round the probability of a win is \(0.6\); otherwise the round is lost. Find the probabilities of exactly six wins; winning more than half the rounds; at least two losses but fewer than five losses; and at least one win together with at least one loss. Give all answers to four decimal places.
starters.hint: Let \(W\sim\mathrm{B}(10,0.6)\). More than half means \(W\ge6\). Convert the stated loss interval using losses equal to \(10-W\). For the final event, exclude only all wins and all losses.
starters.solution:
1. \[P(W=6)=\binom{10}{6}\cdot0.6^6\cdot0.4^4\approx0.2508\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]
  2. \[P(W>5)=1-\sum_{r=0}^{5}\binom{10}{r}\cdot0.6^r\cdot0.4^{10-r}\approx0.6331\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

  3. The allowed loss counts are two, three and four. They correspond to win counts eight, seven and six:

    \[P(2\le\text{losses}<5)=P(6\le W\le8)=\sum_{r=6}^{8}\binom{10}{r}\cdot0.6^r\cdot0.4^{10-r}\approx0.5867\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

  4. All wins and all losses are disjoint. Their complement has both kinds of result:

    \[P(1\le W\le9)=1-0.6^{10}-0.4^{10}\approx0.9938\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

    Subtracting only one extreme would still allow the other. The word “and” requires both a win and a loss.

revision.body:
Check the trial model, define the counted outcome, then translate the event into allowed integer counts.

When is the success count binomial?

Use \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(n,p)\) when there are a fixed number \(n\) of independent trials, each classified as success or failure, with the same success probability \(p\). The variable counts successes, so the count lies in \(0,1,\ldots,n\). “Success” may mean a defect or a loss if that is what is counted.

One ordered pattern versus all permitted orders

\[P(X=r)=\binom{n}{r}p^r(1-p)^{n-r},\qquad r=0,\ldots,n.\]

A particular pattern with \(r\) successes has probability \(p^r(1-p)^{n-r}\). The binomial coefficient chooses the success positions. Include it for any order, but not for one already specified order. Impossible counts have probability zero.

Translate strict and inclusive integer endpoints

\[P(X\ge a)=1-P(X\le a-1),\qquad P(X>a)=1-P(X\le a).\]\[P(a\le X\le b)=P(X\le b)-P(X\le a-1).\]

These bounds use integer \(a,b\). For an open interval, list the included integers first. “At least one” is the complement of zero; “at least two” excludes both zero and one.

Choose a useful count and check the calculation

For a fixed trial total, failures equal \(n-X\); translate both endpoints when changing from one count to the other. Check support, failure probability and exponents summing to \(n\). When removing objects changes the conditional success probability, without-replacement draws do not satisfy the independent constant-probability trial assumptions. Keep full precision until the final rounding step.
revision.checks: • Fixed trial total; independence; constant probability; counted event; position factor; integer bounds; complement; final accuracy.
revision.examTip: Show each method, retain the required precision and state the complete answer.

orig_9709_s1_bg_inverse_binomial.description: Use binomial moments and probability equations to recover parameters, retain every admissible solution, and prove least or greatest integer answers with neighbour checks.

sections.title: How do binomial parameters determine the moments?
sections.label: Binomial moments
sections.intro:
For \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(n,p)\), the success count has mean, variance and standard deviation

\[\mu=np,\qquad v=np(1-p),\qquad \sigma=\sqrt{np(1-p)}.\]

Here \(n\) is a positive integer and \(0\le p\le1\). A standard deviation must be squared before it can be substituted for \(v\).

blocks.html:
For \(0<p<1\), the mean can be obtained directly from the binomial table. Using \(r\binom{n}{r}=n\binom{n-1}{r-1}\), its weighted sum becomes

\[E(X)=np\sum_{s=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{s}p^s(1-p)^{n-1-s}=np.\]

The remaining sum is one by the binomial expansion of \((p+1-p)^{n-1}\).

Similarly, weighting the table by \(r(r-1)\) gives \(n(n-1)p^2\). Since \(r^2=r(r-1)+r\), the second-moment sum is \(n(n-1)p^2+np\). Subtracting the square of the mean gives

\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=n(n-1)p^2+np-n^2p^2=np(1-p).\]

This is a calculation from the finite probability table; the formulas also agree with the constant cases \(p=0\) and \(p=1\).

blocks.title: Stop and think: has the standard deviation been squared?
blocks.prompt: Report A claims a binomial variable has exact mean six and standard deviation two. Report B claims exact mean six and standard deviation three. Find the two variances and identify which report is immediately ruled out by the binomial variance bound.

fields.label: Which report is ruled out by variance exceeding its mean?

blocks.hint: Variance is the square of standard deviation. For a positive binomial mean, the variance is strictly smaller than the mean.
blocks.solution: 1. Report A has variance \(2^2=4<6\). Report B has variance \(3^2=9>6\), so B cannot describe a binomial variable. Checking a necessary bound is not the same as solving all parameters, but it rules out B immediately.

blocks.html: The variance contains the failure probability. For a positive mean, \(p>0\), so \(0\le v<\mu\). A positive variance equal to the mean is not possible for a finite binomial model. When the mean is zero, the variance must also be zero.

sections.title: Can the exact moments recover a valid integer trial count?
sections.label: Recover parameters
sections.intro:
If the exact mean \(\mu\) is positive, divide the variance by the mean:

\[\frac{v}{\mu}=1-p,\qquad p=1-\frac{v}{\mu}.\]

Then recover the trial count from the original mean:

\[n=\frac{\mu}{p}=\frac{\mu^2}{\mu-v}.\]

These formulas require \(\mu>0\) and a resulting positive probability. Check \(0\le v<\mu\) first, then verify that \(n\) is a positive integer and both original moment equations hold.

blocks.title: Use the ratio of exact variance to exact mean
blocks.prompt: A binomial variable has exact mean nine and exact variance six. Recover \(p\) and the positive integer trial count \(n\).
blocks.hint: Because the mean is positive, \(\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{E(X)}=1-p\). Then use the original mean to obtain the trial count.
blocks.solution:
1. \[1-p=\frac{6}{9}=\frac{2}{3},\qquad p=\frac{1}{3},\qquad n=\frac{9}{\frac{1}{3}}=27.\]

  2. The recovered parameters give \(27\cdot\frac{1}{3}=9\) and \(27\cdot\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{2}{3}=6\), so both exact conditions hold.

blocks.html: Do not divide by a zero mean. The ratio \(\frac{v}{\mu}\) is unavailable when \(\mu=0\). Return to \(np=0\) and handle the constant distribution directly. Also distinguish a variance supplied in the question from a supplied standard deviation.

sections.title: Which probability equation determines the unknown parameter?
sections.label: Inverse probabilities
sections.intro:
For a known positive trial count, the no-success event gives

\[P(X=0)=(1-p)^n.\]

If this probability is \(a\), recover the nonnegative failure probability \(1-p=a^{\frac{1}{n}}\), then check \(p\) in its permitted range. With known \(0<p<1\), an unknown trial count may instead be recovered from \(n=\frac{\log(a)}{\log(1-p)}\); an exact equality still requires an admissible integer trial count.

blocks.title: Recover the probability from no successes
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(3,p)\), and suppose \(P(X=0)=\frac{27}{64}\). Find \(p\), then find \(P(X=3)\).
blocks.hint: The cube of the failure probability is \(\frac{27}{64}\). All three successes have probability \(p^3\).

blocks.html:
For \(0<p<1\) and \(0\le r<n\), two consecutive positive binomial terms have ratio

\[\frac{P(X=r+1)}{P(X=r)}=\frac{n-r}{r+1}\cdot\frac{p}{1-p}.\]

This can simplify an inverse calculation because the common powers cancel. Before dividing, check that the denominator is nonzero. An equality between two probabilities may allow endpoint solutions that a defined ratio would exclude.

blocks.title: An exact-count equation can have two interior solutions
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(2,p)\), with \(0\le p\le1\), and suppose \(P(X=1)=\frac{4}{9}\). Find both possible values of \(p\), then identify the one for which the mean exceeds one.
blocks.hint: Use \(2p(1-p)=\frac{4}{9}\). Both roots must be checked before applying the additional mean condition.
blocks.solution:
1. \[2p(1-p)=\frac{4}{9}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad9p^2-9p+2=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(3p-1)(3p-2)=0.\]

  2. Both \(p=\frac{1}{3}\) and \(p=\frac{2}{3}\) are valid. The mean is \(2p\), so the extra condition \(2p>1\) selects \(p=\frac{2}{3}\).

blocks.html: Test every candidate in the original statement. A quadratic exact-count equation can have two interior probability roots. Cancelling a factor can lose valid zero cases, while taking an even root can introduce an inadmissible sign. Apply both the original probability equation and the domain restrictions.

sections.title: Which integer first meets or last meets the requirement?
sections.label: Integer thresholds
sections.intro:
A threshold question asks for a least or greatest integer satisfying a probability requirement. Start with the actual event and preserve whether the inequality is inclusive or strict. For at least one success in \(n\) independent trials,

\[P(X\ge1)=1-(1-p)^n.\]

For \(0<p<1\), this increases with \(n\), while the no-success probability \((1-p)^n\) decreases. These monotonic directions explain which neighbour must fail at a least or greatest answer.

blocks.html: Fourteen is the first passing trial count. The original at-least-one event passes at fourteen and fails at thirteen, proving the least-integer conclusion.

blocks.title: Equality changes a strict integer threshold
blocks.prompt: Independent trials have success probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). Find the least positive integer trial count giving an at-least-one-success probability of at least \(\frac{15}{16}\). Then find the least trial count giving a probability strictly greater than \(\frac{15}{16}\). Also state the probability at four trials.

fields.label: Least n for at least fifteen sixteenths
Least n for strictly more than fifteen sixteenths
Probability of at least one success in four trials

blocks.hint: The probability at \(n\) trials is \(1-(\frac{1}{2})^n\). Check three, four and five trials without rounding the fractions.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P_3(X\ge1)=\frac{7}{8},\qquad P_4(X\ge1)=\frac{15}{16},\qquad P_5(X\ge1)=\frac{31}{32}.\]

  2. The probability increases with the trial count. Four is the first count meeting the inclusive target, while five is the first meeting the strict target. Equality at four cannot be treated as strictly greater.

blocks.html:
The threshold may be a count value rather than the number of trials. For example, if \(Y\sim\mathrm{B}(4,\frac{1}{2})\), the least integer \(k\) satisfying \(P(Y\le k)\ge0.9\) is three because

\[P(Y\le2)=\frac{11}{16}<0.9,\qquad P(Y\le3)=\frac{15}{16}\ge0.9.\]

A cumulative probability is nondecreasing in its count bound, so checking the candidate and the previous bound establishes the minimum.

Use the original event at neighbouring integers. For a minimum, show the candidate passes and the previous integer fails. For a maximum, show the candidate passes and the next integer fails. Near an equality boundary, keep exact values or sufficient precision so that rounding does not change a strict inequality.

Handle endpoint probabilities before logarithms. If \(p=0\), the at-least-one probability is zero for every positive trial count; if \(p=1\), it is one for every positive trial count. For \(0<p<1\), no finite trial count reaches at-least-one probability exactly one. A target of zero or one must therefore be checked directly with its stated inclusive or strict inequality.

sections.title: Are the data exact, admissible and sufficient?
sections.label: Consistency checks
sections.intro: There are three separate checks. First, the moments must be compatible with a probability: for positive mean, \(0\le v<\mu\). Second, the recovered trial count must be an integer. Third, the supplied information must identify the parameters uniquely; constant cases can leave a parameter undetermined.

blocks.html:
With exact mean \(5\), the variance is \(5-\frac{25}{n}\). An exact variance of \(3\) lands at the cross, \(n=\frac{25}{2}\), between the allowed integer points.

Fixing exact mean five gives a discrete set of variances as the integer trial count varies. Exact variance three lies between the values for twelve and thirteen trials and corresponds to the inadmissible real trial count twelve and a half.

blocks.title: Exact and rounded moment data support different conclusions
blocks.prompt: A proposed binomial model has exact mean seven and exact variance three. Find the algebraic values of \(p\) and \(n\), and decide whether an exact model exists. If instead both reported numbers were rounded to the nearest integer, would this calculation alone prove that no binomial model is possible?

fields.label: Does the exact pair define a binomial model?

options.no: No: the recovered trial count is not an integer.
options.yes: Yes: round the recovered trial count.
options.negative: No: the recovered probability is negative.

fields.label: Does the same calculation rule out all models for rounded reports?

options.no: No: the true moments may differ within the rounding intervals.
options.yes: Yes: rounded and exact moment equations are identical.
options.always: No: every pair of rounded numbers must be binomial moments.

blocks.hint: Use the exact recovery formulas for the first part. In the second part, distinguish reported values from the underlying unrounded moments.
blocks.solution:
1. \[p=1-\frac{3}{7}=\frac{4}{7},\qquad n=\frac{7}{\frac{4}{7}}=\frac{49}{4}.\]

    The noninteger trial count rules out the exact pair.

  2. Rounded reports are different. For example, \(\mathrm{B}(12,\frac{3}{5})\) has mean \(\frac{36}{5}=7.2\) and variance \(\frac{72}{25}=2.88\), which round to seven and three. Thus these rounded reports can come from a valid binomial model.

blocks.html: Do not apply an exact rejection to rounded input. If a moment was rounded, its underlying value lies in a rounding interval. Using the displayed number as an exact equality can produce a noninteger trial count even when a valid binomial model exists within the stated accuracy.

In this lesson the trial count is positive. If a different question explicitly allows zero trials, \(n=0\) also gives the constant zero count for any \(p\). State the convention rather than dividing an indeterminate equation or claiming a unique parameter pair.

Conclude with the model status. State the recovered parameters when they are valid, all admissible solutions when there are several, or the exact restriction that rules the model out. For a threshold answer, include the relevant neighbour check as part of the conclusion.

glossary.definition: The expected success count \(np\).
The squared spread \(np(1-p)\) around the mean.
The nonnegative square root of the variance.
A supplied mean or variance treated as an exact value rather than a rounded report.
A parameter satisfying the probability range, integer trial-count requirement and original equations.
A given event probability used to recover an unknown model parameter.
The ratio between probabilities at neighbouring counts, defined only when its denominator is positive.
A least or greatest integer satisfying a specified probability condition.
A calculation showing the proposed integer passes and its relevant adjacent integer fails.
A constant random variable with all probability at a single value and zero variance.

examples.title: Keep mean, variance and standard deviation distinct
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(20,\frac{3}{10})\). Find its mean, variance and standard deviation. Give the standard deviation to three significant figures.
solution:
The mean is the trial count multiplied by the success probability:

\[E(X)=20\cdot\frac{3}{10}=6.\]

The variance includes the additional failure factor:

\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=20\cdot\frac{3}{10}\cdot\frac{7}{10}=\frac{21}{5}=4.2.\]

The standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of the variance:

\[\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{21}{5}}\approx2.05\quad\text{(3 significant figures)}.\]

The mean describes an average count over repeated groups of twenty trials. It does not guarantee six successes in a particular group. The standard deviation is measured in success-count units; the variance uses their square.

examples.title: Recover both parameters from exact positive moments
examples.question: A binomial variable has exact mean six and exact variance \(\frac{9}{2}\). Find its parameters \(n\) and \(p\), and check the recovered model.
solution:
The supplied conditions are

\[np=6,\qquad np(1-p)=\frac{9}{2}.\]

The mean is positive, so divide the variance equation by the mean equation:

\[1-p=\frac{\frac{9}{2}}{6}=\frac{3}{4},\qquad p=\frac{1}{4}.\]

Substitute into the mean equation:

\[n\cdot\frac{1}{4}=6,\qquad n=24.\]

The trial count is a positive integer and the probability is admissible. Check both original conditions:

\[24\cdot\frac{1}{4}=6,\qquad24\cdot\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{9}{2}.\]

Therefore \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(24,\frac{1}{4})\).

examples.title: Use a no-success event to recover the failure probability
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(4,p)\), with \(0\le p\le1\), and suppose \(P(X=0)=\frac{81}{256}\). Find every admissible value of \(p\).
solution:
No successes means that all four trials fail:

\[(1-p)^4=\frac{81}{256}=\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^4.\]
As a real algebraic equation, this permits \(1-p=\frac{3}{4}\) or \(1-p=-\frac{3}{4}\). But a failure probability cannot be negative.

The admissible branch is

\[1-p=\frac{3}{4},\qquad p=\frac{1}{4}.\]

The other branch would give \(p=\frac{7}{4}\), outside the permitted probability range.
Substituting the valid answer gives \((\frac{3}{4})^4=\frac{81}{256}\), exactly as stated. When a root represents a probability, its domain is part of the solution.

examples.title: Check zero-probability endpoints before cancelling a ratio
examples.question:
Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(8,p)\), where \(0\le p\le1\), and suppose

\[P(X=2)=\frac{3}{2}P(X=1).\]

Find all possible values of \(p\). Then explain how the answer changes if the stated information is the defined ratio \(\frac{P(X=2)}{P(X=1)}=\frac{3}{2}\).
solution: Check endpoints before dividing. At \(p=0\), the count is always zero, so both probabilities in the equation are zero. At \(p=1\), the count is always eight, so both are again zero. Thus \(p=0\) and \(p=1\) satisfy the original equality.

For an interior probability \(0<p<1\), both relevant terms are positive. Their ratio simplifies to

\[\frac{P(X=2)}{P(X=1)}=\frac{\binom{8}{2}p^2(1-p)^6}{\binom{8}{1}p(1-p)^7}=\frac{7p}{2(1-p)}.\]

Set this ratio equal to the specified factor:

\[\frac{7p}{2(1-p)}=\frac{3}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad7p=3(1-p)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p=\frac{3}{10}.\]

The complete solution of the original equality is

\[p\in\left\{0,\frac{3}{10},1\right\}.\]

These include the two endpoint solutions that would be lost by dividing by \(P(X=1)\) without checking it.
If the probability ratio itself is given as defined, its denominator must be positive. The endpoint cases then do not qualify, and the unique answer is \(p=\frac{3}{10}\).

examples.title: Find the least trial count and verify the previous integer
examples.question: Independent trials each have success probability \(\frac{1}{5}\). Find the least positive integer \(n\) for which the probability of at least one success is at least \(0.95\).
solution:
Use the no-success complement and preserve the inclusive inequality:

\[1-\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^n\ge0.95\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^n\le0.05.\]

Taking logarithms gives

\[n\log\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)\le\log(0.05).\]

Since \(\log(\frac{4}{5})<0\), division reverses the inequality:

\[n\ge\frac{\log(0.05)}{\log(\frac{4}{5})}\approx13.4251.\]

The candidate least integer is fourteen. Check the original event at fourteen and thirteen:

\[P_{14}(X\ge1)=1-\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{14}=0.95601953488896\ge0.95,\]\[P_{13}(X\ge1)=1-\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{13}=0.9450244186112<0.95.\]

The probability of at least one success increases with \(n\), so all smaller trial counts also fail. Hence the least trial count is \(n=14\). The probability notation here labels which trial count is being used.

examples.title: Find the greatest group size meeting a no-failure requirement
examples.question: Each independently tested item has failure probability \(\frac{1}{50}\). Find the greatest positive integer number \(n\) of tested items for which the probability that none fails is at least \(0.80\).
solution:
A nonfailure has probability \(\frac{49}{50}\), so the required event is

\[P(X=0)=\left(\frac{49}{50}\right)^n\ge0.80,\]

where \(X\) counts failures.

Taking logarithms and dividing by a negative number gives

\[n\log\left(\frac{49}{50}\right)\ge\log(0.80)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n\le\frac{\log(0.80)}{\log(\frac{49}{50})}\approx11.0452.\]

Check the largest candidate integer and the next one:

\[\left(\frac{49}{50}\right)^{11}\approx0.800731\ge0.80,\]\[\left(\frac{49}{50}\right)^{12}\approx0.784717<0.80.\]

The no-failure probability decreases as more items are included. Therefore the greatest permitted group size is \(n=11\). Rounding the real bound to the nearest integer is not the general rule; the direction of the inequality determines which integers are allowed.

examples.title: Audit exact moments, integer trial counts and constant cases
examples.question: Assume the trial count \(n\) is a positive integer. Assess these four proposed pairs of exact binomial moments: A has mean five and variance three; B has mean four and variance five; C has mean zero and variance zero; D has mean four and variance zero.
solution:
For A, positive mean permits the usual division:

\[p=1-\frac{3}{5}=\frac{2}{5},\qquad n=\frac{5}{\frac{2}{5}}=\frac{25}{2}.\]

The probability is valid but the trial count is not an integer. No binomial distribution has exactly this pair of moments. Rounding the trial count would change the moments.

For B, variance exceeds the positive mean. The recovery formula would give

\[p=1-\frac{5}{4}=-\frac{1}{4},\]

which is not a probability. The proposed exact moments are inconsistent.

For C, division by the mean is unavailable. Since \(np=0\) and \(n\) is positive, \(p=0\). Every positive integer \(n\) then gives the same constant count \(X=0\) and variance zero. The moments determine the distribution but do not uniquely determine \(n\).

For D, positive mean and zero variance force \(p=1\). Then \(n=np=4\), so

\[X\sim\mathrm{B}(4,1),\qquad P(X=4)=1.\]

Zero variance is a valid constant case, not automatically an error.

These conclusions use exact supplied moments. If a reported mean or variance has been rounded, apply its stated accuracy or rounding interval before claiming inconsistency; a noninteger answer from rounded numbers is not by itself proof that a binomial model is impossible.

extraPractice.title: Variance and standard deviation are different quantities
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}\left(32,\frac{1}{4}\right)\). Find \(E(X)\), \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) and the exact standard deviation.
extraPractice.hint: Use \(np\) for the mean and \(np(1-p)\) for variance. Take the nonnegative square root only for standard deviation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[E(X)=np=32\cdot\frac{1}{4}=8.\]
  2. \[\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=32\cdot\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=6.\]
  3. \[\sigma=\sqrt{6}.\]

    Using six as the standard deviation would confuse the spread measure with its square.

extraPractice.title: Exact moments require an integer trial total
extraPractice.prompt: A binomial count has exact mean six and exact variance \(\frac{18}{5}\). Find its parameters \(n\) and \(p\). A different proposed binomial count has exact mean nine and exact variance \(\frac{27}{5}\). Decide whether that second model can exist.

fields.label: Can the second exact-moment model exist?

options.yes: Yes, it is a valid binomial model
options.no: No, its exact moments are inconsistent

extraPractice.hint: For a positive mean, divide variance by mean to obtain \(1-p\). Then calculate \(n\) without rounding. A noninteger trial total cannot be repaired when the moments are explicitly exact.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[1-p=\frac{\frac{18}{5}}{6}=\frac{3}{5},\qquad p=\frac{2}{5},\qquad n=6\div\frac{2}{5}=15.\]

    Both parameters are valid, and substituting them gives the stated exact moments.

  2. For the second proposed model,

    \[1-p=\frac{\frac{27}{5}}{9}=\frac{3}{5},\qquad p=\frac{2}{5},\qquad n=9\div\frac{2}{5}=\frac{45}{2}.\]

  3. The resulting trial total is not an integer. No binomial distribution has both of those exact moments. Rounding the trial total would change the moments and would answer a different question.

extraPractice.title: Recover the success probability from no successes
extraPractice.prompt: For \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(5,p)\), it is known that \(P(X=0)=\frac{243}{1024}\). Find \(p\), \(E(X)\) and the exact probability of at least one success.
extraPractice.hint: No successes means five failures. The failure probability belongs to the interval from zero to one, which determines the admissible root.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(1-p)^5=\frac{243}{1024}=\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^5.\]

    As \(1-p\ge0\), this gives \(1-p=\frac{3}{4}\) and \(p=\frac{1}{4}\).

  2. \[E(X)=5\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{5}{4}.\]
  3. \[P(X\ge1)=1-P(X=0)=1-\frac{243}{1024}=\frac{781}{1024}.\]

    The complement includes every positive count, not just exactly one success.

extraPractice.title: A minimum trial total needs the preceding integer checked
extraPractice.prompt: Independent trials each succeed with probability \(0.18\). Find the smallest positive integer number of trials needed so that the probability of at least one success is at least \(0.95\). Also give the at-least-one probabilities at that trial total and at one fewer trial, each to four decimal places.

fields.label: Probability with the chosen trial total

extraPractice.hint: Write the event as the complement of no successes. Taking logarithms gives a real bound, but the answer must be an integer. Use unrounded probabilities to decide which side of the target each neighbour lies on.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[1-0.82^n\ge0.95\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0.82^n\le0.05.\]

  2. Since \(\ln(0.82)<0\), dividing by it reverses the inequality:

    \[n\ge\frac{\ln(0.05)}{\ln(0.82)}\approx15.0956.\]

    The first candidate integer is sixteen.

  3. \[1-0.82^{15}=0.9490425\ldots<0.95,\]\[1-0.82^{16}=0.9582148\ldots\ge0.95.\]

    The probabilities to four decimal places are \(0.9490\) and \(0.9582\).

  4. The at-least-one probability increases with the trial total. Fifteen fails and sixteen passes, so sixteen is the minimum.

extraPractice.title: Zero mean must be treated before division
extraPractice.prompt: Model A is \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(n,p)\), where \(n\) is a positive integer, and it has mean zero. Find \(p\), and decide what the mean tells you about \(n\). Model B is \(Y\sim\mathrm{B}(m,q)\), where \(m\) is a positive integer, and it has exact mean eight and variance zero. Find \(q\) and \(m\).
extraPractice.hint: Start from the original equations. In model A the mean is zero, so variance divided by mean is not a valid operation. In model B the positive mean rules out a zero success probability.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Model A has \(np=0\) with \(n>0\), so \(p=0\). It then always records zero successes and has zero variance for every positive integer \(n\). The trial total is not identified.

  2. Model B satisfies \(mq=8\) and \(mq(1-q)=0\). Substituting the positive mean into the variance equation gives

    \[8(1-q)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q=1,\qquad m=8.\]

  3. This second model always records eight successes. Both endpoint probabilities produce valid constant distributions, but only the positive-mean case determines the trial total here.

extraPractice.title: Recover both binomial parameters
extraPractice.prompt: A binomial variable has mean \(9\) and variance \(6\). Find its trial count and success probability.
extraPractice.hint: Dividing variance by mean gives \(1-p=\frac23\). Then use \(np=9\).
extraPractice.solution:
Dividing variance by mean gives \(1-p=\frac23\). Then use \(np=9\).

  • Trial count: \(27\)
  • Success probability: \(\frac{1}{3}\)

extraPractice.hint: The quadratic is \(p(1-p)=\frac{3}{16}\). Both roots lie strictly between zero and one.
extraPractice.solution:
The quadratic is \(p(1-p)=\frac{3}{16}\). Both roots lie strictly between zero and one.

  • Answer: \(\left\{\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4}\right\}\)

extraPractice.prompt: Each independent trial succeeds with probability \(\frac12\). Find the least trial count for which the chance of at least one success is at least \(\frac78\).

extraPractice.solution:

extraPractice.prompt: Use independent trials with success probability \(\frac12\). Find the least trial count making the chance of at least one success strictly more than \(\frac78\).

starters.title: Recover the model and choose an integer count threshold
starters.question: A binomial random variable \(X\) has exact mean twelve and exact variance nine. Find its parameters \(n\) and \(p\). Then find the smallest integer \(k\) for which \(P(X\le k)\ge0.9\). Give \(P(X\le k-1)\) and \(P(X\le k)\) to four decimal places to justify the threshold. Use the exact binomial model.
starters.hint: Use the moment ratio to recover the model. Evaluate cumulative binomial probabilities at successive integer counts near the required percentile; do not round a continuous approximation into an unverified threshold.
starters.solution:
1. \[1-p=\frac{9}{12}=\frac{3}{4},\qquad p=\frac{1}{4},\qquad n=12\div\frac{1}{4}=48.\]

    The parameters satisfy both exact moment equations.

  2. The exact-model cumulative probability is

    \[P(X\le t)=\sum_{r=0}^{t}\binom{48}{r}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^r\cdot\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{48-r}.\]
  3. \[P(X\le15)=0.8768222\ldots<0.9,\qquad P(X\le16)=0.9295595\ldots\ge0.9.\]

  4. Cumulative probability cannot decrease as the included count increases. Therefore the smallest admissible threshold is \(k=16\). The neighbouring probabilities to four decimal places are \(0.8768\) and \(0.9296\). Their unrounded values establish the inequalities.

starters.title: Use an adjacent-probability relation, then find a maximum
starters.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(10,p)\), where \(0<p<1\), and suppose \(P(X=3)=2P(X=2)\). Find \(p\) and \(E(X)\). A new experiment has \(m\) independent trials with this same success probability. Find the greatest positive integer \(m\) for which the probability of no successes is at least \(0.01\). Give the no-success probabilities at your chosen \(m\) and at \(m+1\), each to four decimal places.
starters.hint: The stated strict probability domain makes \(P(X=2)>0\), so division is valid. After simplifying the adjacent-probability ratio, use the failure probability for the new zero-success event. That event becomes less likely as the trial total grows.
starters.solution:
1. \[\frac{P(X=3)}{P(X=2)}=\frac{\binom{10}{3}}{\binom{10}{2}}\cdot\frac{p}{1-p}=\frac{8}{3}\cdot\frac{p}{1-p}=2.\]

    Thus \(8p=6(1-p)\), giving \(p=\frac{3}{7}\). The initial restriction excludes both degenerate endpoints before this division.

  2. \[E(X)=10\cdot\frac{3}{7}=\frac{30}{7}.\]

  3. The new experiment has zero-success probability \(\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^m\). The required inequality is

    \[\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^m\ge0.01\quad\Longrightarrow\quad m\le\frac{\ln(0.01)}{\ln\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)}\approx8.2292.\]
  4. \[\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^8=0.0113683\ldots\ge0.01,\qquad\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^9=0.0064961\ldots<0.01.\]

    The greatest allowed trial total is eight. The corresponding probabilities to four decimal places are \(0.0114\) and \(0.0065\).

  5. The negative logarithm reverses the inequality when dividing. Checking eight and nine also verifies that the maximum, rather than a minimum, has been chosen.
