revision.body:
Identify the stated moment, keep probability domains, and verify integer boundaries in the original event.

Mean, variance and standard deviation

\[X\sim\mathrm{B}(n,p):\qquad\mu=np,\quad v=np(1-p),\quad\sigma=\sqrt{v}.\]

Square a given standard deviation before using it as variance. For a positive integer trial total, zero mean forces \(p=0\) but does not identify \(n\). Positive mean with zero variance forces \(p=1\), so the mean equals the trial total.

Recover parameters from exact moments

For exact mean \(\mu>0\) and variance \(v\),

\[p=1-\frac{v}{\mu},\qquad n=\frac{\mu}{p}.\]

A valid positive-mean model needs \(0\le v<\mu\) and a positive integer \(n\). Check both original moment equations. Do not round a noninteger trial total into a model with different exact moments. Treat zero mean before any division.

Inverse event equations have domain conditions

\[P(X=0)=(1-p)^n.\]

The failure probability is between zero and one. For \(0<p<1\) and integers \(0\le r<n\), an adjacent-probability ratio simplifies to

\[\frac{P(X=r+1)}{P(X=r)}=\frac{n-r}{r+1}\cdot\frac{p}{1-p}.\]

Use this only when the denominator probability is nonzero. An equality of two zero probabilities can retain endpoint solutions that a defined ratio excludes.

Minimum and maximum integers need neighbour evidence

Translate the requirement using its exact strict or inclusive inequality. Dividing by a negative logarithm reverses the inequality. For a minimum, verify that the chosen integer passes and the previous one fails; for a maximum, verify that the next one fails. For a count percentile, compare consecutive cumulative binomial probabilities. Decide using unrounded values.
revision.checks: • Variance or standard deviation; exact moments; zero-mean case; parameter domains; all roots; integer total; inequality direction; neighbour check.
revision.examTip: Show each method, retain the required precision and state the complete answer.

orig_9709_s1_bg_mixed_binomial.description: Condition count events, build an outer model for independent batches, and distinguish fresh type choices from a shared type or overlapping counts.

sections.title: Which outcomes satisfy both the event and the condition?
sections.label: Conditional binomial
sections.intro:
A binomial model supplies the original count probabilities. Conditioning on an observed count event changes which outcomes remain and how their weights are normalised. For an event \(F\) of positive probability,

\[P(A\mid F)=\frac{P(A\cap F)}{P(F)}.\]

First identify the integer count values satisfying both events. Only their probabilities belong in the numerator. If \(A\) already implies \(F\), the numerator simplifies to \(P(A)\); otherwise it does not.

blocks.title: Stop and think: what belongs in the conditional numerator?
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(4,\frac{1}{2})\). Given \(X\ge2\), find the probability that \(X\le3\). First choose the counts that belong in the numerator.
blocks.hint: The numerator is the intersection of the requested event with the condition. The denominator is the probability of the condition alone.

blocks.html: Do not divide an unfiltered event probability by the condition. Counts excluded by the condition cannot remain in the numerator. A resulting value above one is a warning that the intersection or denominator is wrong.

The conditional count distribution need not itself be binomial with a new success probability. For example, conditioning on at least one success removes zero while retaining several positive counts. Work from the original table and normalise the retained probabilities unless a separate argument establishes another model.

sections.title: What is one trial when the experiment is repeated in batches?
sections.label: Repeated experiments
sections.intro:
One experiment can contain several elementary trials, yet the whole experiment can become one trial of a second count model. Calculate a batch’s qualifying probability \(q\) first. If \(m\) batches are independent and have this same probability, their qualifying count is

\[Y\sim\mathrm{B}(m,q).\]

The outer trial count is the number of batches, and the outer success probability is the probability that a whole batch qualifies.

blocks.title: Find the batch probability before the outer binomial model
blocks.prompt: A batch consists of two independent fair-coin tosses and qualifies if it has exactly one head. Three batches use separate independent tosses. Find the qualifying probability of one batch, the probability that exactly two batches qualify, and the probability that none qualifies.

fields.label: Probability of exactly two qualifying batches

blocks.hint: HT and TH qualify a batch. The outer count has three independent trials, one for each complete batch.
blocks.solution:
1. \[q=\frac{2}{4}=\frac{1}{2},\qquad Y\sim\mathrm{B}\left(3,\frac{1}{2}\right).\]
  2. \[P(Y=2)=\binom{3}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3=\frac{3}{8},\qquad P(Y=0)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3=\frac{1}{8}.\]

blocks.html: Check independence at the level you are counting. Internal trials may be independent within every batch while batches still share a device, hidden type or other common cause. An outer binomial model requires independent batch outcomes, not merely independent trials conditional on a shared state.

A condition on one batch can also change the relevant probability. If only batches satisfying a screening condition are retained, calculate their conditional qualifying probability and specify how the retained batches are sampled before using it in an outer model.

sections.title: Is the type chosen afresh for every independent trial?
sections.label: Fresh type choices
sections.intro:
Suppose each trial independently chooses type A with probability \(w\), or type B with probability \(1-w\). Their success probabilities are \(p_A\) and \(p_B\). The unconditional success probability of one trial is

\[q=wp_A+(1-w)p_B.\]

If both the type choices and outcome-generating randomness are independent across trials, the success indicators are independent with this same \(q\). A fixed count over \(n\) such trials is then \(\mathrm{B}(n,q)\).

blocks.title: Average the trial probability only after checking fresh independence
blocks.prompt: On each of four trials, independently choose type A with probability \(\frac{3}{4}\) or B with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Success probabilities are \(\frac{1}{5}\) for A and \(\frac{3}{5}\) for B. All outcome-generating draws are also independent across trials. Find the unconditional success probability of one trial and the probability that all four trials succeed.
blocks.hint: Weight the two type branches for one trial. The fresh independent choice is repeated, so the resulting success indicators are independent.
blocks.solution:
1. \[q=\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{3}{5}=\frac{3}{10}.\]
  2. \[P(\text{four successes})=\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)^4=\frac{81}{10000}.\]

blocks.html: State what is independently repeated. The complete type-choice-and-outcome procedure must restart on each trial. A one-trial weighted average alone does not justify a binomial count if one selected type is retained for the whole batch.

sections.title: Is one selected type shared by the entire batch?
sections.label: Shared-type mixtures
sections.intro:
Now choose one type and retain it for all \(n\) trials. Conditional on A, the success count is \(\mathrm{B}(n,p_A)\); conditional on B, it is \(\mathrm{B}(n,p_B)\). Weight the two complete count distributions:

\[P(M=r)=w\binom{n}{r}p_A^r(1-p_A)^{n-r}+(1-w)\binom{n}{r}p_B^r(1-p_B)^{n-r}.\]

The original choice weight is applied once per batch. An observation of the count can then update the probability of which type was selected.

blocks.title: One shared type changes both the count probability and the posterior
blocks.prompt: Choose A once with probability \(\frac{3}{4}\), or B once with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Retain it for two trials, independent conditional on the selected type. Success probabilities are \(\frac{1}{5}\) for A and \(\frac{3}{5}\) for B. Find the probability of two successes and the posterior probability of B given two successes. Then find the two-success probability if a fresh type were instead independently chosen on each trial.

fields.label: Two-success probability with one shared type
Probability of B given two successes
Two-success probability with fresh independent choices

blocks.hint: For a shared type, weight the two complete two-trial paths. For fresh choices, first obtain the unconditional one-trial success probability.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(\text{two successes})=\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{25}+\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{9}{25}=\frac{3}{25}.\]
  2. \[P(B\mid\text{two successes})=\frac{\frac{9}{100}}{\frac{3}{25}}=\frac{3}{4}.\]

  3. The fresh-choice success probability is \(\frac{3}{10}\), so two fresh independent successes have probability \((\frac{3}{10})^2=\frac{9}{100}\). The posterior in the shared experiment differs from B’s original selection probability \(\frac{1}{4}\).

blocks.html:
Both counts have mean \(\frac74\). The shared-type count has more mass at the extremes and larger variance, \(\frac{17}{16}\) compared with \(\frac{35}{48}\).

Fresh choices and one shared choice have the same one-trial success probability and count mean in this example. Their full count distributions and variances differ because a shared type links the outcomes within a batch.

blocks.title: A shared-type mixture can match a binomial mean but differ in spread
blocks.prompt: A type is selected once with equal probabilities. Its success probability is either \(\frac{1}{4}\) or \(\frac{3}{4}\), and two trials are independent conditional on that type. The resulting count \(M\) has probabilities \(\frac{5}{16},\frac{3}{8},\frac{5}{16}\) at zero, one and two. Find its mean and variance, then compare its tail masses with \(\mathrm{B}(2,\frac{1}{2})\).

options.tails: The mixture has more probability at both zero and two.
options.same: The complete distributions are identical because their means match.
options.centre: The mixture has more probability at one and less at both extremes.

blocks.hint: Use the supplied mixture table for both moments. The comparison binomial probabilities at zero and two are each \(\frac{1}{4}\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[E(M)=1\cdot\frac{3}{8}+2\cdot\frac{5}{16}=1,\qquad E(M^2)=1\cdot\frac{3}{8}+4\cdot\frac{5}{16}=\frac{13}{8}.\]
  2. \[\operatorname{Var}(M)=\frac{13}{8}-1^2=\frac{5}{8}.\]

    Both extreme probabilities \(\frac{5}{16}\) exceed \(\frac{1}{4}\), despite the common mean of one. The mixture is not the stated binomial distribution.

blocks.html: Conditional independence is not unconditional independence. Knowing the type can make the trials independent within that branch. When the shared type is unknown, an early success provides information about that type and can change the probability of later successes.

The distinction need not produce different count distributions in every boundary case. If both types have the same success probability, or only one type can be selected, the two constructions agree. A batch of one trial also has the same one-trial distribution under either procedure. Check the actual structure and parameters rather than assuming every mixture must differ.

sections.title: Which underlying trials do the two counts share?
sections.label: Joint counts
sections.intro: To use a product of two count probabilities, justify independence of the counts themselves. Counts based on disjoint groups of mutually independent trials are independent. Counts that reuse trials or share a selected type need a joint model; their separate marginal binomial distributions are not enough.

blocks.html:
Two overlapping head counts

In three independent fair tosses, \(U\) counts the heads in tosses 1 and 2 and \(V\) counts the heads in tosses 2 and 3. Each inner cell gives the joint probability for its pair of counts.

Count \(U\)\(V=0\)\(V=1\)\(V=2\)Row total
\(U=0\)\(\tfrac18\)\(\tfrac18\)\(0\)\(\tfrac14\)
\(U=1\)\(\tfrac18\)\(\tfrac28\)\(\tfrac18\)\(\tfrac12\)
\(U=2\)\(0\)\(\tfrac18\)\(\tfrac18\)\(\tfrac14\)
Column total\(\tfrac14\)\(\tfrac12\)\(\tfrac14\)\(1\)

The row \(U=0\) gives \(P(V=0\mid U=0)=\dfrac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}}=\dfrac12\).

The joint probability \(\frac18\) differs from the product \(\frac14\times\frac14=\frac1{16}\), so the two counts are dependent. Each count individually follows \(\mathrm{B}(2,\frac12)\).

Both counts have binomial marginal distributions, but the middle toss belongs to both. The joint table exposes the dependence and provides the correct row total for conditioning.

blocks.title: Different outcome-category counts from the same trials are linked
blocks.prompt: Four fair-die rolls are independent. Let \(R\) count ones and \(S\) count twos in those same four rolls. Find \(P(R=0,S=0)\) and \(P(R=1,S=1)\), then decide whether the two counts are independent.

fields.label: Probability of neither ones nor twos
Probability of one one and one two

options.no: No: the same rolls constrain both counts.
options.yes: Yes: all underlying die rolls are independent.
options.equal: Yes: both individual counts have the same binomial distribution.

blocks.hint: A roll that is neither a one nor a two has probability \(\frac{4}{6}\). For one of each, choose the position of the one and then a different position for the two; the other positions must be neither.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(R=0,S=0)=\left(\frac{4}{6}\right)^4=\frac{16}{81}.\]
  2. \[P(R=1,S=1)=4\cdot3\cdot\frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{1}{6}\left(\frac{4}{6}\right)^2=\frac{4}{27}.\]

  3. The two counts are linked because a roll cannot be both a one and a two. For example, \(R=4\) forces \(S=0\), whereas the unconditional probability of \(S=0\) is only \((\frac{5}{6})^4\). Independent die rolls do not make these two counts from the same rolls independent.

blocks.html: Build the joint event from the elementary outcomes. For overlapping counts, enumerate the underlying outcomes, condition on the shared trials, or count allowed position patterns. Merge all paths producing the same pair before conditioning or summing over a total.

Even for independent counts, different success probabilities can prevent the combined total from having a single standard binomial model. You can always sum disjoint joint cases when independence is justified, but combining the totals into one binomial count also needs a common success probability across the underlying trials.

Separate three operations. Multiply probabilities for independent joint conditions, add probabilities for disjoint alternative cases, and divide a joint probability by a positive conditioning probability. State which operation the model justifies at each step.

glossary.definition: A count-event probability calculated within an observed event of positive probability.
A model counting qualifying outcomes across independent repetitions of a complete batch experiment.
The probability that one entire batch meets the stated criterion.
An independently repeated type selection before each trial.
One initially selected type retained for all trials in a batch.
A full count distribution formed by weighting the distributions from the possible selected types.
The updated probability of a selected type after observing a count.
The distribution of one count obtained by summing the joint table over the other count.
A table assigning a probability to every permitted pair of count values.
Counts that reuse some of the same underlying trial outcomes.

examples.title: Intersect the count events before dividing
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(5,\frac{1}{3})\). Given that at least one success occurred, find the probability of exactly two successes and the probability of at most two successes.
solution:
The condition is \(F=\{X\ge1\}\), with probability

\[P(F)=1-\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^5=\frac{211}{243}.\]

Exactly two successes already satisfy the condition. The numerator is therefore

\[P(X=2)=\binom{5}{2}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^3=\frac{80}{243}.\]

Hence

\[P(X=2\mid X\ge1)=\frac{\frac{80}{243}}{\frac{211}{243}}=\frac{80}{211}.\]

For at most two, the intersection with the condition is \(1\le X\le2\), not \(X\le2\). The additional allowed value has probability

\[P(X=1)=5\cdot\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^4=\frac{80}{243}.\]

\[P(X\le2\mid X\ge1)=\frac{P(X=1)+P(X=2)}{P(X\ge1)}=\frac{160}{211}.\]

The count zero must not be included in this conditional numerator.

examples.title: Treat a complete independent batch as one outer trial
examples.question: A batch consists of three independent fair-coin tosses. A batch qualifies if it contains exactly two heads. Four batches use separate tosses, and all twelve tosses are independent. Let \(Y\) count qualifying batches. Find its distribution, the probability of exactly two qualifying batches, and the probability of at least one.
solution:
First calculate the probability that one batch qualifies:

\[q=\binom{3}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3=\frac{3}{8}.\]

At the outer level, one trial is one whole batch. There are four independent batches with the same qualifying probability, so

\[Y\sim\mathrm{B}\left(4,\frac{3}{8}\right).\]

Exactly two qualifying batches have probability

\[P(Y=2)=\binom{4}{2}\left(\frac{3}{8}\right)^2\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)^2=\frac{675}{2048}.\]

The complement of at least one qualifying batch is that all four fail to qualify:

\[P(Y\ge1)=1-\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)^4=\frac{3471}{4096}.\]

Counting heads across all twelve tosses is a different variable. A group with three heads does not qualify, while a group with exactly two does. The outer binomial probability is the qualifying probability of a batch, not the head probability of one toss.

examples.title: A fresh independent type choice can produce an ordinary binomial count
examples.question: On each of three trials, choose a fresh type: A with probability \(\frac{1}{3}\), or B with probability \(\frac{2}{3}\). A trial of type A succeeds with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\); a trial of type B succeeds with probability \(\frac{3}{4}\). Type choices and the outcome-generating random draws are independent across trials. Let \(F\) count successes. Find its distribution and the probability of three successes.
solution:
The two type branches give the one-trial success probability

\[q=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{4}+\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{7}{12}.\]

The full type-and-outcome experiment is independently repeated on every trial. Thus the three success indicators are independent with the same probability \(q\), giving

\[F\sim\mathrm{B}\left(3,\frac{7}{12}\right).\]

The complete table, useful for later comparison, is

\(f\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(P(F=f)\)\(\frac{125}{1728}\)\(\frac{525}{1728}\)\(\frac{735}{1728}\)\(\frac{343}{1728}\)
The probabilities total one. It is the fresh independent repetition of the whole selection procedure that justifies using the averaged one-trial probability in a binomial model.

examples.title: One shared type requires a weighted mixture and a posterior update
examples.question: Choose type A once with probability \(\frac{1}{3}\), or type B once with probability \(\frac{2}{3}\), and retain that type for all three trials. Conditional on the selected type, the trial outcomes are independent. Success probabilities are \(\frac{1}{4}\) for A and \(\frac{3}{4}\) for B. Let \(M\) count successes. Construct its distribution and find the probability that B was selected given three successes.
solution:
Within each fixed type, the count is binomial. The conditional distributions are

\(m\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(P(M=m\mid A)\)\(\frac{27}{64}\)\(\frac{27}{64}\)\(\frac{9}{64}\)\(\frac{1}{64}\)
\(m\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(P(M=m\mid B)\)\(\frac{1}{64}\)\(\frac{9}{64}\)\(\frac{27}{64}\)\(\frac{27}{64}\)

Weight each complete table by its initial type probability, then add matching counts. For example,

\[P(M=2)=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{9}{64}+\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{27}{64}=\frac{63}{192}.\]

The full mixture is

\(m\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(P(M=m)\)\(\frac{29}{192}\)\(\frac{45}{192}\)\(\frac{63}{192}\)\(\frac{55}{192}\)

Three successes arise through A with joint weight \(\frac{1}{192}\) and through B with joint weight \(\frac{54}{192}\). Therefore

\[P(B\mid M=3)=\frac{\frac{54}{192}}{\frac{55}{192}}=\frac{54}{55}.\]

The prior probability of B was \(\frac{2}{3}\), but three successes favour the type with the larger success probability. The posterior must use the total probability of three successes in the denominator.

Each individual trial still has success probability \(\frac{7}{12}\), but the outcomes share the same selected type. Their unconditional independence is not justified. In particular,

\[P(M=3)=\frac{55}{192}\ne\left(\frac{7}{12}\right)^3.\]

examples.title: Compare moments using the two complete count tables
examples.question: Compare the fresh-type count \(F\) from Worked example 3 with the shared-type count \(M\) from Worked example 4. In both experiments, A has selection probability \(\frac{1}{3}\) and success probability \(\frac{1}{4}\), while B has selection probability \(\frac{2}{3}\) and success probability \(\frac{3}{4}\). Use their complete three-trial count tables to calculate each mean and variance.
solution:
The two distributions, with each probability attached to the same count value, are

\(f\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(P(F=f)\)\(\frac{125}{1728}\)\(\frac{525}{1728}\)\(\frac{735}{1728}\)\(\frac{343}{1728}\)
\(m\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(P(M=m)\)\(\frac{29}{192}\)\(\frac{45}{192}\)\(\frac{63}{192}\)\(\frac{55}{192}\)

For the fresh-type model, direct weighted sums give

\[E(F)=\frac{525+2\cdot735+3\cdot343}{1728}=\frac{7}{4},\]\[E(F^2)=\frac{525+4\cdot735+9\cdot343}{1728}=\frac{91}{24},\]\[\operatorname{Var}(F)=\frac{91}{24}-\left(\frac{7}{4}\right)^2=\frac{35}{48}.\]

For the shared-type model, use its own table throughout:

\[E(M)=\frac{45+2\cdot63+3\cdot55}{192}=\frac{7}{4},\]\[E(M^2)=\frac{45+4\cdot63+9\cdot55}{192}=\frac{33}{8},\]\[\operatorname{Var}(M)=\frac{33}{8}-\left(\frac{7}{4}\right)^2=\frac{17}{16}.\]

The means match, but the shared-type count has the larger variance: \(\frac{17}{16}>\frac{35}{48}\). Selecting a high- or low-success type once makes the entire batch more likely to contain many or few successes.

A binomial count over three trials with mean \(\frac{7}{4}\) would have success probability \(\frac{7}{12}\), and variance \(\frac{35}{48}\). It cannot reproduce the shared-type table’s variance \(\frac{17}{16}\). Matching a one-trial probability or a mean alone does not establish the binomial count model.

examples.title: Disjoint groups of independent trials give independent counts
examples.question: Five fair-coin tosses are independent. Let \(U\) count heads in the first three tosses and \(V\) count heads in the last two. Find \(P(U=2,V\ge1)\) and \(P(U+V=3)\).
solution: The two counts use disjoint groups of the independent tosses. Hence \(U\sim\mathrm{B}(3,\frac{1}{2})\) and \(V\sim\mathrm{B}(2,\frac{1}{2})\), and these counts are independent.

For the first event, multiply the two count-event probabilities:

\[P(U=2,V\ge1)=\frac{3}{8}\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{4}\right)=\frac{9}{32}.\]

For a total of three heads, the possible count pairs are \((1,2),(2,1),(3,0)\). These joint cases are disjoint:

\[P(U+V=3)=\frac{3}{8}\cdot\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{8}\cdot\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{8}\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{5}{16}.\]

There is also a direct check: \(U+V\) counts heads across all five independent fair tosses, so its distribution is \(\mathrm{B}(5,\frac{1}{2})\). Thus

\[P(U+V=3)=\binom{5}{3}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^5=\frac{5}{16}.\]

This direct binomial model is justified by the underlying five trials, all with the same success probability.

examples.title: A shared trial can make two binomial counts dependent
examples.question: Three fair-coin tosses are independent. Let \(U\) count heads in tosses one and two, and let \(V\) count heads in tosses two and three. Find their joint distribution, \(P(U=0,V=0)\) and \(P(V=0\mid U=0)\). Decide whether the counts are independent.
solution: Each marginal count has distribution \(\mathrm{B}(2,\frac{1}{2})\), but both include toss two. Enumerate the eight equally likely three-toss strings and map each string to its pair \((U,V)\).

The strings TTT, TTH, THT, THH, HTT, HTH, HHT and HHH produce pairs \((0,0),(0,1),(1,1),(1,2),(1,0),(1,1),(2,1),(2,2)\). Combining repeated pairs gives

\(P(U=u,V=v)\)\(v=0\)\(v=1\)\(v=2\)Row total
\(u=0\)\(\frac{1}{8}\)\(\frac{1}{8}\)\(0\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)
\(u=1\)\(\frac{1}{8}\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)\(\frac{1}{8}\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)
\(u=2\)\(0\)\(\frac{1}{8}\)\(\frac{1}{8}\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)
Column total\(\frac{1}{4}\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)\(1\)

Both counts equal zero exactly when all three tosses are tails:

\[P(U=0,V=0)=\frac{1}{8}.\]

But the product of the marginal probabilities is

\[P(U=0)P(V=0)=\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{16}.\]

These differ, so the counts are not independent.

Condition within the row \(U=0\):

\[P(V=0\mid U=0)=\frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{1}{2}.\]

Knowing \(U=0\) already tells us that toss two was tails. Only the third toss then decides whether \(V=0\).

Some individual pairs can happen to satisfy a product equality. For example, \(P(U=1,V=1)=\frac{1}{4}\) equals \(P(U=1)P(V=1)\), but that single agreement does not establish independence. Independence must hold for every joint pair.

extraPractice.title: Condition on at least one success
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}\left(4,\frac{1}{3}\right)\). Find \(P(X\ge1)\), \(P(X=2\mid X\ge1)\) and \(P(X\ge3\mid X\ge1)\). Give exact answers.
extraPractice.hint: Calculate the probability of the given event first. Each requested numerator lies wholly inside that event, but it still needs division by the conditioning probability.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(X\ge1)=1-\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^4=1-\frac{16}{81}=\frac{65}{81}.\]
  2. \[P(X=2)=\binom{4}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\cdot\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2=\frac{24}{81}.\]

    Therefore

    \[P(X=2\mid X\ge1)=\frac{24}{81}\div\frac{65}{81}=\frac{24}{65}.\]
  3. \[P(X\ge3)=\binom{4}{3}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^3\cdot\frac{2}{3}+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^4=\frac{9}{81},\]\[P(X\ge3\mid X\ge1)=\frac{9}{81}\div\frac{65}{81}=\frac{9}{65}.\]

    The conditional table on counts one through four is renormalized; it is not obtained simply by deleting zero and leaving every other probability unchanged.

extraPractice.title: A whole batch becomes one outer success
extraPractice.prompt: A batch contains three devices. Each independently fails inspection with probability \(0.1\). A batch is labelled bad if at least one device fails. Five batches are inspected, with all device outcomes independent across and within batches. Find the probability that one batch is bad, the trial total in the binomial model for the number of bad batches, and the probability that exactly two of the five batches are bad. Give the final probability to four decimal places.

fields.label: Probability that one batch is bad

extraPractice.hint: First calculate one batch’s event probability. In the second model, a success is a bad batch, so its probability is not the original device failure probability.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[q=P(\text{bad batch})=1-0.9^3=0.271.\]

  2. The five batch indicators are independent with the same probability \(q\), so for their count \(Y\),

    \[Y\sim\mathrm{B}(5,0.271).\]

    The outer trial total is five batches, not fifteen devices.

  3. \[P(Y=2)=\binom{5}{2}\cdot0.271^2\cdot0.729^3\approx0.2845\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

extraPractice.title: Fresh type choices and one shared choice are different models
extraPractice.prompt: Type A has success probability \(0.8\); type B has success probability \(0.2\). Types are chosen with equal probabilities. In the fresh-choice experiment, a new type is chosen independently before each of four trials, and all trial generation is independent. In the shared-choice experiment, one type is chosen once and used for all four trials, whose outcomes are independent conditional on that type. Is the fresh-choice success count \(\mathrm{B}\left(4,\frac{1}{2}\right)\)? Find the probability of four successes in each experiment. Is the shared-choice count also \(\mathrm{B}\left(4,\frac{1}{2}\right)\)?

fields.label: Fresh-choice count has the stated binomial model
Four successes with one shared choice
Shared-choice count has the stated binomial model

extraPractice.hint: Both experiments have the same marginal success probability on one trial. Only the fresh experiment also has independent trials after the type labels are forgotten. For the shared experiment, weight the four-success probability within each fixed-type branch.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(\text{success on one trial})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot0.8+\frac{1}{2}\cdot0.2=\frac{1}{2}.\]

    Independent fresh choices and independent trial generation give the binomial model with four trials and probability \(\frac{1}{2}\).

  2. \[P(\text{four successes, fresh})=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4=\frac{1}{16}.\]
  3. \[P(\text{four successes, shared})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot0.8^4+\frac{1}{2}\cdot0.2^4=\frac{257}{1250}.\]

  4. The shared result differs from \(\frac{1}{16}\), so the claimed binomial model is false. The fixed hidden type links the four trials even though they are independent when that type is known.

extraPractice.title: A posterior needs the full observed-event denominator
extraPractice.prompt: Choose coin A with probability \(\frac{3}{5}\), otherwise choose coin B. Their head probabilities are respectively \(\frac{1}{4}\) and \(\frac{3}{4}\). Toss the chosen coin three times independently conditional on the choice. Let \(X\) be the number of heads. Find \(P(X=2)\), \(P(B\mid X=2)\), \(P(X\ge1)\) and \(P(B\mid X\ge1)\).
extraPractice.hint: Multiply the conditional binomial probability by the initial coin-choice probability to get a joint branch weight. The denominator of a posterior includes all initial branches capable of producing the observed event.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(A\text{ and }X=2)=\frac{3}{5}\cdot\binom{3}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{27}{320},\]\[P(B\text{ and }X=2)=\frac{2}{5}\cdot\binom{3}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{54}{320}.\]
  2. \[P(X=2)=\frac{81}{320},\qquad P(B\mid X=2)=\frac{54}{320}\div\frac{81}{320}=\frac{2}{3}.\]
  3. \[P(X=0)=\frac{3}{5}\cdot\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^3+\frac{2}{5}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^3=\frac{83}{320},\]\[P(X\ge1)=1-\frac{83}{320}=\frac{237}{320}.\]

  4. The B-branch joint probability for at least one head is

    \[\frac{2}{5}\cdot\left[1-\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^3\right]=\frac{126}{320}.\]

    Hence

    \[P(B\mid X\ge1)=\frac{126}{320}\div\frac{237}{320}=\frac{42}{79}.\]

extraPractice.title: A sum of independent counts is an event over count pairs
extraPractice.prompt: Independent random variables satisfy \(X\sim\mathrm{B}\left(3,\frac{1}{2}\right)\) and \(Y\sim\mathrm{B}\left(4,\frac{1}{4}\right)\). Find \(P(X=1,Y=2)\), \(P(X+Y=2)\) and the probability that both counts are positive.
extraPractice.hint: Independence permits multiplication of a probability about X and a probability about Y. For a fixed sum, add the disjoint pairs of counts producing that sum. Their unequal success probabilities prevent pooling them using one common trial probability.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(X=1)=\frac{3}{8},\qquad P(Y=2)=\binom{4}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2\cdot\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2=\frac{27}{128}.\]\[P(X=1,Y=2)=\frac{3}{8}\cdot\frac{27}{128}=\frac{81}{1024}.\]

  2. The pairs giving total two are \((0,2),(1,1),(2,0)\). Thus

    \[P(X+Y=2)=\frac{1}{8}\cdot\frac{27}{128}+\frac{3}{8}\cdot\frac{27}{64}+\frac{3}{8}\cdot\frac{81}{256}=\frac{621}{2048}.\]
  3. \[P(X\ge1,Y\ge1)=\left(1-\frac{1}{8}\right)\cdot\left(1-\frac{81}{256}\right)=\frac{7}{8}\cdot\frac{175}{256}=\frac{1225}{2048}.\]

    The two original counts are independent by assumption. That is the reason the separate event probabilities can be multiplied.

extraPractice.title: Add the routes for one success
extraPractice.prompt: Two independent attempts have success probabilities \(\frac13\) and \(\frac14\). Find the probability of exactly one success.
extraPractice.hint: Add the two orders in which exactly one attempt succeeds.
extraPractice.solution:
Add the two orders in which exactly one attempt succeeds.

  • Answer: \(\frac{5}{12}\)

extraPractice.title: Condition on the shared machine
extraPractice.prompt: Choose A or B with equal probability, then use that machine for both trials. The trials are independent given the machine, with success probability \(\frac12\) on A and \(\frac14\) on B. Find the probability both trials succeed.
extraPractice.hint: Square each machine's success probability before averaging the two results.
extraPractice.solution:
Square each machine's success probability before averaging the two results.

  • Answer: \(\frac{5}{32}\)

extraPractice.title: Choose the batch success event
extraPractice.prompt: Two independent devices each fail with probability \(\frac14\). A batch fails when either device fails. Find the batch failure probability.
extraPractice.hint: Use the complement of both devices passing.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the complement of both devices passing.

  • Answer: \(\frac{7}{16}\)

extraPractice.title: Condition on a nonzero count
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm B(2,\frac14)\). Find \(\mathrm P(X=2\mid X>0)\).
extraPractice.hint: Divide the probability of two successes by the probability of at least one.
extraPractice.solution:
Divide the probability of two successes by the probability of at least one.

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{7}\)

starters.title: A batch event becomes an outer model and an inner condition
starters.question: Each batch contains four independent trials, each successful with probability \(0.2\). A batch qualifies if it contains exactly two successes. Eight batches are run, with all trial outcomes independent across batches. Let \(Y\) be the number of qualifying batches. Find the exact qualification probability for one batch and \(E(Y)\). Find \(P(Y=1)\) and \(P(Y\ge2)\), each to four decimal places. For one specified batch, given that it qualifies, find the probability that its first trial succeeded.
starters.hint: Use a four-trial binomial calculation to obtain one qualification probability, then an eight-trial binomial count of qualifying batches. For the final conditional question, return to one batch and count its success-position patterns.
starters.solution:
1. \[q=\binom{4}{2}\cdot0.2^2\cdot0.8^2=0.1536=\frac{96}{625}.\]

    The independent batches have a common qualification probability, so \(Y\sim\mathrm{B}\left(8,\frac{96}{625}\right)\).

  2. \[E(Y)=8\cdot\frac{96}{625}=\frac{768}{625}.\]
  3. \[P(Y=1)=8\cdot0.1536\cdot0.8464^7\approx0.3824\quad\text{(4 d.p.)},\]\[P(Y\ge2)=1-0.8464^8-8\cdot0.1536\cdot0.8464^7\approx0.3542\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

  4. Within a qualifying batch, the six choices of two success positions are equally likely. Exactly three include the first position:

    \[P(\text{first trial succeeds}\mid\text{exactly two successes})=\frac{\binom{3}{1}}{\binom{4}{2}}=\frac{1}{2}.\]

  5. The original trial probability \(0.2\) is not the probability after learning that this particular four-trial batch contains exactly two successes.

starters.title: The same one-trial success rate does not fix the joint model
starters.question: Machine A produces a successful result with probability \(0.9\); machine B does so with probability \(0.6\). A machine choice selects A with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\) and B with probability \(\frac{3}{5}\). Compare two procedures for three trials. In procedure F, a new machine is independently chosen before each trial and all trial generation is independent. In procedure S, one machine is chosen once for all three trials, which are independent conditional on the machine. Find the common marginal success probability on one trial. Find the probability of exactly two successes under F and under S, each to four decimal places. Under S, find the exact probability that A was chosen given exactly two successes.
starters.hint: Procedure F has independent fresh choices and therefore a binomial count using the marginal probability. Procedure S needs two separately weighted binomial branches. Its posterior numerator is the A-branch joint probability.
starters.solution:
1. \[p=\frac{2}{5}\cdot0.9+\frac{3}{5}\cdot0.6=0.72=\frac{18}{25}.\]

  2. Under F, \(X_F\sim\mathrm{B}(3,0.72)\), so

    \[P(X_F=2)=\binom{3}{2}\cdot0.72^2\cdot0.28\approx0.4355\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

  3. Under S, the joint contributions are

    \[P(A\text{ and }X_S=2)=\frac{2}{5}\cdot\binom{3}{2}\cdot0.9^2\cdot0.1=0.0972,\]\[P(B\text{ and }X_S=2)=\frac{3}{5}\cdot\binom{3}{2}\cdot0.6^2\cdot0.4=0.2592.\]

    Adding them gives \(P(X_S=2)=0.3564\).

  4. \[P(A\mid X_S=2)=0.0972\div0.3564=\frac{3}{11}.\]

  5. Both procedures have the same one-trial marginal probability, but their three-trial distributions differ. Averaging success probabilities before using the binomial formula is justified for the independent fresh choices, not for the shared hidden machine.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: compute the common marginal success probability.
  • 1 mark: identify why independent fresh choices give a binomial model.
  • 1 mark: form the fresh-procedure exactly-two probability.
  • 1 mark: obtain its value to the requested accuracy.
  • 1 mark: form the A-branch joint contribution under the shared procedure.
  • 1 mark: form the B-branch joint contribution.
  • 1 mark: add both contributions for the shared observed-event probability.
  • 1 mark: retain the A joint weight as the posterior numerator.
  • 1 mark: obtain the exact posterior.
  • 1 mark: distinguish conditional independence within a fixed machine from marginal independence after hiding the machine choice.

revision.body:
Identify what is conditioned on, what is repeated independently, and whether a hidden type is chosen afresh or shared.

The conditional numerator is an intersection

\[P(E\mid F)=\frac{P(E\cap F)}{P(F)},\qquad P(F)>0.\]

Translate both events into allowed integer counts before evaluating their intersection. Normalize by the whole given event. Conditioning a success count does not automatically create another binomial model with a smaller trial total.

An independent batch event can become an outer success

First calculate \(q\), the probability that one batch meets the required event. If \(N\) batches are independent and identically generated, the number meeting that event has

\[Y\sim\mathrm{B}(N,q).\]

The outer probability is the batch event probability, not the original single-trial probability. A hidden state shared across batches can invalidate the required independence.

Fresh and shared type choices must be distinguished

Independent fresh type choices before every trial give marginal probability

\[p_*=wp_A+(1-w)p_B.\]

When the trials are also generated independently, their count is binomial with \(p_*\). For one type shared across the whole experiment, calculate each conditional binomial table and mix it with the initial branch weights. For a posterior, divide the chosen branch’s joint weight by the full observed-event weight.

Joint counts require the actual dependence structure

For independent counts,

\[P(X=r,Y=s)=P(X=r)P(Y=s).\]

For a fixed sum, add the disjoint count pairs giving that sum. Do not average unequal trial probabilities to claim one binomial model for the full combined trial count. Counts sharing trials, or sharing a hidden type, need their true joint sample space; marginal binomial labels alone do not imply independence.
revision.checks: • Intersection; nonzero condition; inner event; outer trial total; independent batches; fresh or shared type; joint weight; overlap.
revision.examTip: Show each method, retain the required precision and state the complete answer.

orig_9709_s1_bg_geometric.description: Count the successful trial, distinguish first-success events from survival tails, and use memorylessness and the mean to solve waiting-time questions.

sections.title: What is repeated, and exactly what does the waiting variable count?
sections.label: Geometric assumptions
sections.intro:
A geometric trial-count model describes repeated independent trials with the same success probability \(p\), continued until the first success. The recorded variable includes the successful trial:

\[X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(p).\]

For \(0<p<1\), its support is \(1,2,3,\ldots\). Unlike a fixed-trial binomial count, it records how long the experiment waits for its first success.

Define one trial, define success, check independence and constant probability, and check that there is no finite stopping cap. A draw without replacement from a small fixed-composition bag generally changes the success probability and needs its own model.

blocks.title: Stop and think: does the recorded count include the success?
blocks.prompt: A bag contains two green and three white tokens. Draw uniformly, replace and mix after every failure, and stop at the first green. Successive draws are independent. Lara counts every draw including the final green; Liam counts only the whites before it. Which record uses the geometric trial-count convention, what is its success probability, and what is its smallest possible value?

fields.label: Which record counts trials through success?

options.lara: Lara’s count, including the successful draw.
options.both: Both records have the same values and probabilities.

blocks.hint: A green on the very first draw gives Lara one and Liam zero. Replacement keeps the same success probability on every continuing draw.
blocks.solution: 1. Lara’s count has distribution \(\mathrm{Geo}(\frac{2}{5})\) on \(1,2,3,\ldots\). Liam’s failure count is one less. The final successful draw is included in the convention used here.

blocks.html: Include the success in the count. First success on trial \(r\) means \(r-1\) failures followed by one success. A failure-only count starts at zero and has shifted event boundaries; it is a different recording convention.

At \(p=1\), success is certain on the first trial, so \(X=1\) with probability one. At \(p=0\), no success can ever occur: there is no first-success distribution supported on \(1,2,\ldots\). Handle these cases directly instead of inserting undefined expressions into a formula.

sections.title: Which unique success/failure pattern gives the first success?
sections.label: First-success probabilities
sections.intro:
Write \(q=1-p\) for the failure probability. For \(0<p<1\), first success on trial \(r\) requires \(r-1\) failures in their specified positions, then success:

\[P(X=r)=q^{r-1}p=(1-p)^{r-1}p,\qquad r=1,2,3,\ldots.\]

No ordering coefficient is needed because the first success has a prescribed position. There is no earlier success to place elsewhere.

blocks.title: Distinguish a first success from three initial failures
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(\frac{1}{3})\). Find the probability that the first success is on trial four, and the probability that the first three trials all fail.

fields.label: Probability of first success on trial four

blocks.hint: The first event specifies FFFS. The second specifies only FFF and leaves the next trial unrestricted.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(X=4)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^3\cdot\frac{1}{3}=\frac{8}{81},\]
  2. \[P(X>3)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^3=\frac{8}{27}.\]

    The final success factor belongs only in the first calculation.

blocks.html:
Which trials are fixed?

Let \(X\) count trials up to and including the first success, where \(p=\frac14\) and \(q=\frac34\). S means success, F means failure and a dot leaves the outcome unrestricted.

EventFirst five trialsProbability
\(X=5\)F F F F S\(q^4p=\tfrac{81}{1024}\)
\(X>4\)F F F F ·\(q^4=\tfrac{81}{256}\)
\(X\geq4\)F F F · ·\(q^3=\tfrac{27}{64}\)

For the last event, a success on trial 4 is allowed. Only the first three failures enter the product.

First success on trial five requires four failures and a success. Waiting beyond four requires only those four failures, while waiting at least four requires only the first three failures.

A finite display of the first \(N\) probabilities is not the complete distribution. Their total and the missing tail are

\[\sum_{r=1}^{N}P(X=r)=1-q^N,\qquad P(X>N)=q^N.\]

Keep that remaining tail visible. Dividing the displayed probabilities by their subtotal would instead produce the conditional distribution given \(X\le N\), which is a different question.

A display limit is not a stopping rule. Showing the first ten waiting values does not mean the experiment ends after ten failures. A process that actually stops at a finite cap must account for the no-success outcome at that cap separately.

sections.title: How many failures do the tail and interval events require?
sections.label: Tails and memorylessness
sections.intro:
For a positive integer \(k\),

\[P(X>k)=q^k,\qquad P(X\ge k)=q^{k-1}.\]

The first event needs \(k\) initial failures. The second needs only \(k-1\), because success on trial \(k\) is allowed. Consequently,

\[P(X\le k)=1-q^k,\qquad P(X<k)=1-q^{k-1}.\]

For integers \(1\le a\le b\), an inclusive interval is

\[P(a\le X\le b)=q^{a-1}-q^b.\]

List the included trial numbers when the bounds are strict or noninteger rather than applying an endpoint rule mechanically.

blocks.title: Translate the waiting interval into survival probabilities
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(\frac{1}{5})\). Find \(P(X\ge4)\), \(P(X>4)\), and \(P(2<X\le5)\).

fields.label: Probability of waiting at least four trials
Probability of waiting more than four trials
Probability of first success on trial three, four or five

blocks.hint: At least four needs three failures; more than four needs four failures. The interval is longer than two trials but not longer than five.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(X\ge4)=\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^3=\frac{64}{125},\qquad P(X>4)=\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^4=\frac{256}{625}.\]
  2. \[P(2<X\le5)=P(X>2)-P(X>5)=\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^2-\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^5=\frac{976}{3125}.\]

blocks.html:
For \(0<p<1\), known failures do not change the distribution of the future independent trials. For nonnegative integers \(s,t\), the condition \(X>s\) has positive probability and

\[P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=\frac{q^{s+t}}{q^s}=q^t.\]

This equals the probability of needing more than \(t\) trials in a fresh run. It concerns the additional wait after the known failures, not the original total trial number.

After three known failures, the next trial is the first additional trial. The two bars at each count coincide. In particular, \(P(X>5\mid X>3)=P(X>2)=\frac9{16}\).

After three known failures, the fourth trial is the first additional trial. The remaining wait has the same geometric probabilities as a fresh run; two more failures have probability nine sixteenths.

blocks.title: Restart the remaining-wait count after known failures
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(\frac{1}{3})\). Given that the first four trials failed, find the probability of waiting beyond trial six and the probability that the first success is exactly on trial six.

fields.label: Probability of waiting beyond six given waiting beyond four
Probability of first success on six given waiting beyond four

blocks.hint: The fifth trial is the first additional trial. Beyond six needs two further failures; success exactly on six needs failure followed by success.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(X>6\mid X>4)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2=\frac{4}{9},\]
  2. \[P(X=6\mid X>4)=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{9}.\]

    The condition has positive probability \((\frac{2}{3})^4\), so both conditional probabilities are defined.

blocks.html: Check the conditioning event and restart the additional count correctly. After \(s\) failures, trial \(s+1\) is additional trial one. If a proposed condition has probability zero, its conditional probability is undefined; for example, at \(p=1\), even one observed failure is impossible.

sections.title: What does the reciprocal mean tell us about waiting?
sections.label: Geometric mean
sections.intro:
For the geometric trial-count convention,

\[E(X)=\frac{1}{p}.\]

One way to see this is to add the chances that each trial is needed. Trial one is always needed, trial two is needed after one failure, trial three after two failures, and so on:

\[E(X)=1+q+q^2+\cdots=\frac{1}{1-q}=\frac{1}{p}.\]

For \(0<p<1\), this geometric series converges. The constant case \(p=1\) gives mean one directly.

blocks.title: Recover the trial probability from the exact expected wait
blocks.prompt: A geometric trial-count variable has exact mean \(\frac{10}{3}\). Find the success probability and \(P(X>2)\). After five known failures, what is the expected number of additional trials through the first success?

fields.label: Probability of waiting more than two trials
Expected number of additional trials after five failures

blocks.hint: Use the reciprocal relation between mean and success probability. Memorylessness concerns the additional wait, whose count restarts at the next trial.
blocks.solution:
1. \[p=\frac{1}{E(X)}=\frac{3}{10},\qquad P(X>2)=\left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^2=\frac{49}{100}.\]

  2. Five failures have positive probability. The additional waiting time still has geometric parameter \(\frac{3}{10}\), so its mean remains \(\frac{10}{3}\). This answer counts future trials, not the five already completed.

blocks.html: Invert an exact expected wait to recover the success probability. If the exact mean is \(\mu\), then \(p=\frac{1}{\mu}\). A finite geometric trial-count mean must be at least one. An expected value below one is incompatible with a variable whose supported trial counts all begin at one.

A smaller positive success probability gives a longer expected wait, but individual runs remain variable. Memorylessness does not mean the experiment has no history; it means that known failures provide no change to the future trial probabilities under the independent, constant-probability model.

sections.title: Can the probability or confidence requirement determine the waiting model?
sections.label: Inverse waiting
sections.intro:
A tail probability often determines the parameter directly. If \(P(X>k)=a\) for a positive integer \(k\), then the failure probability satisfies

\[q^k=a,\qquad q=a^{\frac{1}{k}},\qquad p=1-a^{\frac{1}{k}}.\]

Use the nonnegative probability root and check the original event. An exact first-success probability, such as \(P(X=2)\), can instead give a quadratic with more than one valid probability.

blocks.title: Use an inverse tail and preserve a strict confidence boundary
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(p)\), and suppose \(P(X>2)=\frac{1}{4}\). Find \(p\). Then find the least positive integer \(m\) for which \(P(X\le m)\ge\frac{7}{8}\), and the least for which \(P(X\le m)>\frac{7}{8}\).

fields.label: Least trial bound for the inclusive target
Least trial bound for the strict target

blocks.hint: The failure probability is the nonnegative square root of \(\frac{1}{4}\). Check the exact within-trial probabilities at two, three and four.
blocks.solution:
1. \[(1-p)^2=\frac{1}{4},\qquad1-p=\frac{1}{2},\qquad p=\frac{1}{2}.\]
  2. \[P(X\le2)=\frac{3}{4},\qquad P(X\le3)=\frac{7}{8},\qquad P(X\le4)=\frac{15}{16}.\]

  3. The first inclusive solution is three, but equality at three does not meet the strict target. Its first solution is four.

blocks.html: Retain all admissible probability roots and verify the integer boundary. A trial bound must be a positive integer. For a least bound, show that it passes the original probability target and that the preceding integer fails. If the target is strict, equality at a candidate does not qualify.

The event “first success within \(m\) trials” is the same underlying event as “at least one success in the first \(m\) trials”. This explains the common complement \(1-(1-p)^m\) in geometric waiting and fixed-trial binomial questions, even though the random variables record different things.

For \(0<p<1\), no finite trial bound guarantees a success with probability exactly one. At \(p=1\), one trial is sufficient. At \(p=0\), a positive-probability success target cannot be reached. Check these endpoints before taking logarithms.

glossary.definition: The number of independent constant-probability trials through and including the first success.
A successful trial preceded only by failures.
The number of failures before the first success, which is one less than the trial count.
The probability that the first success has not yet occurred by a specified trial.
The number of further trials through success after some failures are already known.
The remaining wait after known failures has the same distribution as the initial wait under independent constant-probability trials.
The geometric trial-count mean \(\frac{1}{p}\).
The probability beyond the last value shown in a finite display of an infinite distribution.
A trial bound whose within-bound success probability meets a specified target.
The success probability on each trial; it must be positive for a first-success model on the positive integers.

examples.title: Count every trial through the first success
examples.question: A fair die with faces numbered one to six is rolled independently until the first six appears. Let \(X\) be the number of rolls made, including that final roll. State its distribution and possible values. Explain how \(X\) differs from the number of non-six rolls before the first six.
solution: One trial is one roll, and success means a six. Trials are independent and the success probability is constant at \(p=\frac{1}{6}\). The experiment continues until the first success.

Using the trial-count convention,

\[X\sim\mathrm{Geo}\left(\frac{1}{6}\right),\qquad X\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\}.\]

A success on the first roll gives \(X=1\), not zero.

If \(Y\) counts only the failures before the first success, then \(Y=X-1\) and its values start at zero. For instance, the sequence failure, failure, success gives \(X=3\) and \(Y=2\). Keep the variable definition visible before choosing an exponent.

There is no fixed maximum number of rolls. The chance of still having no six after \(m\) rolls is \((\frac{5}{6})^m\), which tends to zero as \(m\) grows. The first success occurs eventually with probability one, although any particular finite waiting time can be exceeded.

examples.title: The first success at five is one specified stopping pattern
examples.question: Independent trials each succeed with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Let \(X\) count the trials through the first success. Find \(P(X=5)\), and explain why no combination factor is needed.
solution: The event \(X=5\) requires the exact pattern FFFFS: the first four trials fail and the fifth succeeds.
The success position is fixed by the phrase “first success on trial five”. There is only one permitted success/failure pattern, so no combination factor is added.

Exactly one success somewhere among five trials is a different event: it allows five success positions. A first-success question fixes all earlier trials as failures and fixes the final trial as success.

examples.title: Strict and inclusive waiting tails differ by one failure
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(\frac{1}{4})\), counting the successful trial. Find \(P(X>4)\), \(P(X\ge4)\), and \(P(4\le X\le6)\).
solution:
To wait more than four trials, all of the first four trials must fail. There is no requirement on the fifth trial:

\[P(X>4)=\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^4=\frac{81}{256}.\]

To wait at least four trials, only the first three must fail. The fourth may be the successful trial:

\[P(X\ge4)=\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^3=\frac{27}{64}.\]

The interval includes first success on trials four, five or six. Start with all waits of at least four and remove waits longer than six:

\[P(4\le X\le6)=P(X\ge4)-P(X>6)\]\[=\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^3-\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^6=\frac{999}{4096}.\]
The exponents count failed trials, not the endpoint numbers automatically. In the interval calculation, the lower event needs three failures, while the excluded upper tail needs six failures.

examples.title: After known failures, count the additional wait from the next trial
examples.question: Independent trials succeed with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Let \(X\) count trials through the first success. Given that the first three trials failed, find \(P(X>5\mid X>3)\) and \(P(X=5\mid X>3)\). Describe the distribution of the additional waiting time.
solution:
The condition is \(X>3\), with positive probability \((\frac{3}{4})^3\). Waiting beyond trial five means two further failures:

\[P(X>5\mid X>3)=\frac{(\frac{3}{4})^5}{(\frac{3}{4})^3}=\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2=\frac{9}{16}.\]

First success on trial five, after the known first three failures, needs one more failure on trial four followed by success on trial five:

\[P(X=5\mid X>3)=\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{16}.\]

Within the condition, define \(T=X-3\) as the number of additional trials through success. Its values begin at one, because trial four is the first additional trial. Independence and unchanged success probability give

\[T\mid(X>3)\sim\mathrm{Geo}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right).\]
The three failures are known history; they do not make success more likely on the next independent trial. This unchanged distribution of the remaining wait is the memoryless property.

examples.title: An expected waiting time is an average, not a deadline
examples.question: Independent attempts succeed with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\), and attempts continue until the first success. Find the expected number of attempts. Does the answer imply that success must occur within three attempts?
solution:
The trial-count variable has geometric mean

\[E(X)=\frac{1}{p}=\frac{1}{\frac{2}{5}}=\frac{5}{2}.\]
The mean is two and a half attempts across repeated independent runs of the experiment. Individual runs use an integer number of attempts; an expected value need not itself be a possible count.

Waiting longer than three attempts remains possible:

\[P(X>3)=\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^3=\frac{27}{125}>0.\]

Thus the expected wait is not a maximum or a guarantee about one run.

After any specified number of failures, the expected number of additional attempts is still \(\frac{5}{2}\), provided the conditioning event has positive probability. The completed attempts are not included again in that additional-wait variable.

examples.title: An inverse first-success probability may have two admissible roots
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(p)\), counting the successful trial, and suppose \(P(X=2)=\frac{2}{9}\). Find all possible values of \(p\). Then select the value consistent with \(P(X>1)>\frac{1}{2}\).
solution:
First success on trial two requires one failure and then success:

\[(1-p)p=\frac{2}{9}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad9p^2-9p+2=0.\]

\[(3p-1)(3p-2)=0,\qquad p=\frac{1}{3}\quad\text{or}\quad p=\frac{2}{3}.\]

Both values lie in the geometric parameter range and reproduce the given probability.

The additional condition concerns a failed first trial:

\[P(X>1)=1-p>\frac{1}{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p<\frac{1}{2}.\]

It therefore selects \(p=\frac{1}{3}\).
An exact first-success probability need not determine one parameter by itself. Keep both admissible roots until an extra condition distinguishes them.

examples.title: Prove the least number of trials needed for a confidence target
examples.question: Each independent trial succeeds with probability \(\frac{1}{5}\). Find the least positive integer \(m\) such that the first success occurs within \(m\) trials with probability at least \(0.99\).
solution:
“Within \(m\) trials” includes a first success on trial \(m\). Its complement is failure on all of the first \(m\) trials:

\[P(X\le m)=1-\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^m\ge0.99.\]

Rearrange and take logarithms:

\[\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^m\le0.01,\qquad m\ge\frac{\log(0.01)}{\log(0.8)}\approx20.6377.\]

The inequality reverses when dividing by the negative logarithm.

The candidate is twenty-one. Check it and the preceding integer in the original event:

\[P(X\le20)=1-\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{20}\approx0.988471<0.99,\]\[P(X\le21)=1-\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{21}\approx0.990777\ge0.99.\]
The within-trial probability increases with \(m\), so twenty fails along with every smaller value, while twenty-one passes. The least required trial count is \(m=21\).

related.title: Repeated successes and mixed stopping rules

extraPractice.title: The variable must count trials until a first success
extraPractice.prompt:
Decide whether a geometric distribution on positive integers models each stated variable.

A: Independent trials each succeed with probability \(0.3\); \(X\) is the trial number of the first success.

B: A bag contains two target counters and six other counters, drawn uniformly without replacement; \(X\) is the draw number of the first target.

C: Twelve independent trials each succeed with probability \(0.3\); \(X\) is the number of successes.

D: Independent trials each have success probability zero; \(X\) is claimed to have a finite first-success trial number.
extraPractice.hint: A geometric first-success model uses independent trials with the same positive success probability and counts the successful trial itself. Check both the experiment and the meaning of the recorded variable.
extraPractice.solution:
1. A: yes. The trials are independent with constant positive probability \(0.3\), and \(X\) counts trials up to and including the first success.

  2. B: no. Removing non-target counters changes the next target probability. The first-target position also has a finite maximum of seven in this experiment.

  3. C: no. The number of trials is fixed and \(X\) counts successes, so the stated count is binomial rather than a first-success waiting time.

  4. D: no. With success probability zero, success never occurs. There is no proper probability distribution for a finite first-success trial number on \(1,2,\ldots\).

extraPractice.title: Surviving to a trial is different from succeeding on it
extraPractice.prompt: Independent trials each succeed with probability \(\frac{2}{7}\). Let \(X\) count trials up to and including the first success. Find \(P(X=1)\), \(P(X=4)\), \(P(X\ge4)\) and \(P(X>4)\).
extraPractice.hint: Success on trial four requires three failures followed by a success. Requiring at least four trials needs only three initial failures; more than four trials needs four failures.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(X=1)=\frac{2}{7}.\]

    There are no failures before an immediate first success.

  2. \[P(X=4)=\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)^3\cdot\frac{2}{7}=\frac{250}{2401}.\]
  3. \[P(X\ge4)=\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)^3=\frac{125}{343},\qquad P(X>4)=\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)^4=\frac{625}{2401}.\]

  4. The exact-four probability is the difference between these tails: needing at least four trials but not needing more than four.

extraPractice.title: An interval removes the correct survival tail
extraPractice.prompt: The first-success trial number \(X\) has success probability \(\frac{2}{5}\) on every independent trial. Find \(P(3\le X\le6)\), \(P(3<X\le6)\) and \(P(X>7\mid X>3)\).
extraPractice.hint: For the inclusive interval, keep all first successes from trial three onwards and remove those after trial six. For the strict lower endpoint, require three initial failures instead of two. The condition in the last part records three known failures.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(3\le X\le6)=P(X\ge3)-P(X>6)=\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^2-\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^6=\frac{4896}{15625}.\]
  2. \[P(3<X\le6)=P(X>3)-P(X>6)=\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^3-\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^6=\frac{2646}{15625}.\]

  3. The conditioning event has positive probability. Its required continuation is four further failures:

    \[P(X>7\mid X>3)=\frac{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^7}{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^3}=\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^4=\frac{81}{625}.\]

    The additional waiting period has not lasted seven new trials; three failures are already known.

extraPractice.title: A fractional mean is not a possible fractional trial
extraPractice.prompt: Independent attempts each succeed with probability \(0.08\), and \(X\) is the first-success attempt number. Find \(E(X)\) exactly. Then find \(P(X\le E(X))\) and \(P(X>E(X))\), each to four decimal places.
extraPractice.hint: The mean may be noninteger even though individual trial numbers are integers. Translate the event involving the mean into the largest or smallest allowed integer trial number.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[E(X)=\frac{1}{0.08}=\frac{25}{2}=12.5.\]

    This is an average waiting time, not a possible half-trial result or a guaranteed completion time.

  2. Since \(X\) is integer, \(X\le12.5\) means \(X\le12\). Therefore

    \[P(X\le E(X))=1-0.92^{12}\approx0.6323\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

  3. The complementary event \(X>12.5\) is \(X\ge13\), equivalent to twelve initial failures:

    \[P(X>E(X))=0.92^{12}\approx0.3677\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

extraPractice.title: Inverse survival and the certain-success endpoint
extraPractice.prompt: Model A is a geometric first-success model with unknown success probability \(p\), and \(P(X>3)=\frac{8}{27}\). Find \(p\) and \(E(X)\). In a separate model B the success probability is one. Find the probability that its first success is on trial one and its expected first-success trial number.

fields.label: Expected trial number in model A
Probability of trial-one success in model B
Expected trial number in model B

extraPractice.hint: Survival beyond trial three means three failures, so solve for a failure probability in the interval from zero to one. Handle certain success directly rather than conditioning on an impossible earlier failure.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(1-p)^3=\frac{8}{27}=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad1-p=\frac{2}{3},\qquad p=\frac{1}{3}.\]
  2. \[E(X)=\frac{1}{p}=3.\]

  3. For model B, the first trial succeeds with certainty. Its first-success variable equals one with probability one, and its mean is one. An event requiring an earlier failure has probability zero and cannot be used as a conditioning event.

extraPractice.title: Count the earlier failures
extraPractice.prompt: Independent trials succeed with probability \(\frac14\). Find the probability the first success occurs on trial three.
extraPractice.hint: Two failures precede the success on the third trial.
extraPractice.solution:
Two failures precede the success on the third trial.

  • Answer: \(\frac{9}{64}\)

extraPractice.title: Translate the waiting tail
extraPractice.prompt: For a geometric waiting time \(T\) with success probability \(\frac12\), find \(\mathrm P(T>4)\).
extraPractice.hint: The first four trials must all fail.
extraPractice.solution:
The first four trials must all fail.

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{16}\)

extraPractice.title: Recover the trial probability
extraPractice.prompt: For a geometric waiting time \(T\), the ratio \(\frac{\mathrm P(T=3)}{\mathrm P(T=2)}\) is \(\frac23\). Find the trial success probability.
extraPractice.hint: The extra failure factor is \(1-p=\frac23\).
extraPractice.solution:
The extra failure factor is \(1-p=\frac23\).

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{3}\)

extraPractice.title: Combine both routes into the cap
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(W=\min(T,4)\), where \(T\) is the first success with probability \(\frac14\) per independent trial. Find \(\mathrm P(W=4)\).
extraPractice.hint: Every wait of at least four contributes to the cap. Only the first three failures are required.
extraPractice.solution:
Every wait of at least four contributes to the cap. Only the first three failures are required.

  • Answer: \(\frac{27}{64}\)

starters.title: One first-success probability can identify two models
starters.question: Independent trials each succeed with probability \(p\), where \(0<p\le1\), and \(X\) is the first-success trial number. It is known that \(P(X=2)=\frac{3}{16}\). Find both possible values of \(p\), giving the smaller and larger separately. You are then told that \(E(X)<3\). Identify the remaining value of \(p\), and find the exact probability that the first success occurs within the first three trials under this model.
starters.hint: The second trial is the first success only if the first trial fails and the second succeeds. Solve the resulting quadratic completely, then apply the additional mean condition to both candidates.
starters.solution:
1. \[(1-p)p=\frac{3}{16}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad16p^2-16p+3=0,\]\[(4p-1)(4p-3)=0.\]

    The two admissible candidates are \(p=\frac{1}{4}\) and \(p=\frac{3}{4}\); both lie in the stated probability domain.

  2. Their expected first-success trial numbers are respectively four and \(\frac{4}{3}\). Only the latter is strictly less than three, so the additional condition selects \(p=\frac{3}{4}\).

  3. \[P(X\le3)=1-\left(1-\frac{3}{4}\right)^3=1-\frac{1}{64}=\frac{63}{64}.\]

    The first probability equation alone was insufficient to choose between the two models.

  • 1 mark: form the correct quadratic.

starters.title: Check the deadline and then reset only the additional wait
starters.question: Independent trials each succeed with probability \(0.12\), and \(X\) counts trials up to the first success. Find the smallest positive integer \(m\) such that \(P(X\le m)\ge0.98\). Give \(P(X\le m-1)\) and \(P(X\le m)\), each to four decimal places, to justify your answer. Separately, given that the first five trials have failed, find the probability that the first success occurs within the next three trials, also to four decimal places.
starters.hint: Completion by trial m is the complement of m failures. After five known failures, the future trials retain their original independent success probability, and only three additional trials belong in the continuation calculation.
starters.solution:
1. \[1-0.88^m\ge0.98\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0.88^m\le0.02.\]

    As \(\ln(0.88)<0\),

    \[m\ge\frac{\ln(0.02)}{\ln(0.88)}\approx30.6025.\]
  2. \[P(X\le30)=1-0.88^{30}=0.9783986\ldots<0.98,\]\[P(X\le31)=1-0.88^{31}=0.9809908\ldots\ge0.98.\]

    The completion probability increases with the trial number, so \(m=31\) is the minimum. The neighbouring values to four decimal places are \(0.9784\) and \(0.9810\).

  3. The separate conditional event is \(5<X\le8\), given \(X>5\). The conditioning event has probability \(0.88^5>0\):

    \[P(X\le8\mid X>5)=\frac{0.88^5-0.88^8}{0.88^5}=1-0.88^3\approx0.3185\quad\text{(4 d.p.)}.\]

  4. The five known failures do not make the next trial more likely to succeed. They change the original trial labels, while the additional waiting distribution retains the same success probability.

  • 1 mark: form the required probability inequality.
  • 1 mark: use logarithms with the correct inequality direction.
  • 1 mark: identify the candidate integer deadline.
  • 1 mark: verify that the preceding integer fails using an unrounded probability.
  • 1 mark: verify that the chosen integer succeeds and justify minimality.
  • 1 mark: give both neighbour probabilities at the requested accuracy.
  • 1 mark: translate the continuation into three additional trials after five known failures.
  • 1 mark: use a valid conditional ratio or memorylessness with a nonzero conditioning probability.
  • 1 mark: obtain the continuation probability to the requested accuracy.

revision.body:
Count the successful trial itself: a first success on trial \(r\) means exactly \(r-1\) preceding failures.

First-success assumptions and endpoints

Trials must be independent with the same success probability \(p\). The variable records a positive trial number, including the successful trial. For \(0<p<1\), any positive integer is possible. If \(p=1\), the variable is certainly one. If \(p=0\), no finite first success occurs, so there is no proper positive-integer waiting distribution.

Exact success, strict survival and an interval

For \(0<p<1\), put \(q=1-p\). For integers \(r\ge1\) and \(1\le a\le b\),

\[P(X=r)=q^{r-1}p,\qquad P(X>r)=q^r.\]\[P(X\ge r)=q^{r-1},\qquad P(a\le X\le b)=q^{a-1}-q^b.\]

Only the exact first-success event includes a final success factor. Handle the certain-success endpoint directly.

Expected wait and the additional wait after failures

\[E(X)=\frac{1}{p},\qquad0<p\le1.\]

The mean need not be a whole number and is not a maximum wait. For \(0<p<1\) and nonnegative integers \(s,t\),

\[P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=q^t.\]

The condition has positive probability. Known failures leave the additional independent trials unchanged; keep original and additional trial numbers distinct.

Inverse probabilities and integer completion thresholds

Solve the event equation within \(0<p\le1\) and check every candidate. A given probability such as \(P(X=2)=p(1-p)\) may allow two models. For completion by trial \(m\), use \(P(X\le m)=1-q^m\). Reverse the inequality when dividing by \(\ln q<0\); then check the candidate integer and its neighbour in the original event, before rounding.
revision.checks: • Successful trial included; constant probability; first \(r-1\) failures; strict endpoint; conditional event possible; additional wait; all roots; neighbour check.

orig_9709_s1_bg_success_sequences.description: Count the position of a later success, restart independent waits correctly, and build complete finite tables when a target competes with a stopping cap.

sections.title: Where must the final required success occur?
sections.label: Later successes
sections.intro:
For independent trials with constant success probability \(p\), let \(T_r\) be the trial on which the \(r\)th success occurs. Here \(r\) is a positive integer. To have \(T_r=n\), trial \(n\) must succeed and the first \(n-1\) trials must contain exactly \(r-1\) successes. For \(0<p<1\) and integer \(n\ge r\), elementary position counting gives

\[P(T_r=n)=\binom{n-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^{n-r}.\]

The coefficient chooses only the earlier success positions. For \(n<r\), the event is impossible. When \(r=1\), this reduces to the first-success geometric probability.

blocks.html:
