For independent trials with \(p=\frac13\), all five patterns have the same probability. Therefore \[P(T_2=6)=\binom51\left(\frac13\right)^2\left(\frac23\right)^4=\frac{80}{729}.\]

The final trial is fixed as a success. Choose the single earlier success from the first five positions; each of the five patterns contains two successes and four failures.

blocks.title: Stop and think: which success positions are still free?
blocks.prompt: Independent fair trials have success probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). To obtain the third success on trial seven, which condition is needed? Choose it, then find the number of permitted patterns and the probability.

fields.label: Which event fixes the correct first-completion time?

options.prefix: Exactly two successes among trials one to six, followed by success on trial seven.
options.anywhere: Exactly three successes anywhere among seven trials.
options.early: At least three successes among trials one to six.

fields.label: Probability of third success on trial seven

blocks.hint: The final success position is fixed. Choose the two earlier success positions from the first six.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\binom{6}{2}=15,\qquad P(T_3=7)=15\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^7=\frac{15}{128}.\]

    The prefix has only two successes, so none of these paths reaches the third success prematurely.

blocks.html: First completion fixes the final success. The preceding prefix must be below the target, not merely have a suitable total by the end. Counting all arrangements of \(r\) successes among \(n\) trials does not identify the trial of the \(r\)th success.

At \(p=1\), the \(r\)th success occurs deterministically at trial \(r\). At \(p=0\), no positive success target is reached in a finite time. These endpoint cases should be handled directly rather than through an ambiguous zero-power expression.

sections.title: Does the process genuinely restart with independent trials?
sections.label: Fresh waits
sections.intro:
After a success in an independent constant-probability sequence, the next trial starts a fresh wait for the next success. The successful trial already completed is not counted again. If every new trial has the same probability and is independent of the past, the successive waits have the same geometric trial-count distribution and are independent.

A restart can also introduce a new trial probability, provided the new experiment is explicitly independent. In that case each wait uses its own parameter. A retained hidden type or a changing physical state must be accounted for before multiplying waiting probabilities.

blocks.title: Separate two independent waits and add the possible total-time cases
blocks.prompt: A first independent trial sequence has success probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). After its first success, a new trial sequence with success probability \(\frac{1}{2}\) begins, independent of all first-stage outcomes. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) count trials through the first success in their respective stages. Find \(P(X=2,Y=1)\) and \(P(X+Y=3)\).

fields.label: Probability of the stated pair of waits
Probability of a total of three trials

blocks.hint: The joint wait uses a first-stage failure then success and an immediate second-stage success. Total three has the disjoint pairs \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\).

blocks.html: Define each time variable separately. “The second success occurs on trial five” refers to a total position. “The second wait lasts five trials” begins after the first success. Write the possible pairs of positive waits before summing a total-time event.

sections.title: What event makes the experiment reach its final permitted trial?
sections.label: Finite caps
sections.intro:
A capped first-success experiment stops at the first success or after a fixed positive integer cap \(N\). For positive \(p\), if \(X\) is the uncapped first-success time, its actual trial count is \(T=\min(X,N)\). For \(0<p<1\) and \(N\ge2\),

\[P(T=t)=(1-p)^{t-1}p\quad(1\le t<N),\]\[P(T=N)=(1-p)^{N-1}.\]

The final event requires only the first \(N-1\) failures. It includes success on trial \(N\) and failure on every one of the \(N\) trials.

blocks.html: At the cap, stopping time four merges a success on trial four with four failures. Their weights add to eight twenty-sevenths; neither terminal history may be omitted.

blocks.title: Split the final cap mass before asking about completion
blocks.prompt: Independent trials succeed with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Stop at the first success or after three trials, and let \(T\) be the number of trials made. Find the probability of making three trials, the probability of first success on trial three, the probability of no success at all, and the success probability conditional on making three trials.

fields.label: Probability of success on the last trial
Success probability given three trials were made

blocks.hint: Reaching the third trial requires only the first two failures. Then the third trial either succeeds or fails.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(T=3)=\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2=\frac{9}{16},\]
  2. \[P(\mathrm{FFS})=\frac{9}{16}\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{9}{64},\qquad P(\mathrm{FFF})=\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^3=\frac{27}{64}.\]
  3. \[P(\text{success}\mid T=3)=\frac{\frac{9}{64}}{\frac{9}{16}}=\frac{1}{4}.\]

blocks.html: Reaching the cap does not mean failure. A target can be completed on the final permitted trial. Track the pair “stopping time and completion status” before combining histories into the stopping-time table.

Endpoint rules remain meaningful for the capped experiment. With \(p=0\), exactly \(N\) trials are made and no success occurs, even though an uncapped first-success time has no distribution on positive integers. With \(p=1\), a first-success experiment stops at one. If \(N=1\), it always makes one trial, with success or failure still distinguished by that trial’s result.

sections.title: Which terminal histories give the same time or reward?
sections.label: Finite distributions
sections.intro:
A bounded stopping process has a finite set of terminal histories. First assign each history its actual probability. Then map it to the recorded variable: number of trials, reward, final score or completion status. Histories with the same variable value must have their probabilities added.

Calculate moments from the complete resulting table:

\[E(Z)=\sum_z zP(Z=z),\qquad E(Z^2)=\sum_z z^2P(Z=z),\]\[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=E(Z^2)-[E(Z)]^2.\]

For a capped waiting variable, use its finite stopping table rather than an uncapped geometric mean.

blocks.title: Use every stopping-time row in the moment calculation
blocks.prompt: A stopping time \(T\) takes values one, two and three with probabilities \(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{4}\). Find its mean and variance from the full table.
blocks.hint: Find the weighted mean and the weighted second moment separately before subtracting the square of the mean.
blocks.solution:
1. \[E(T)=1\cdot\frac{1}{2}+2\cdot\frac{1}{4}+3\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{7}{4},\]
  2. \[E(T^2)=1^2\cdot\frac{1}{2}+2^2\cdot\frac{1}{4}+3^2\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{15}{4},\]
  3. \[\operatorname{Var}(T)=\frac{15}{4}-\left(\frac{7}{4}\right)^2=\frac{11}{16}.\]

blocks.html: The recorded variable determines which paths combine. Two histories can share a stopping time but have different completion status or reward. A time-only table is sufficient for time moments, but it may be insufficient for a reward or conditional-completion question.

An early terminal path is weighted only through its actual final trial. For example, a first-toss head in the three-toss reward game has probability \(\frac{1}{2}\), not \(\frac{1}{8}\). Later tosses are not performed; a full-length enumeration is valid only if all irrelevant continuations are summed consistently.

sections.title: Which rule stops the path first?
sections.label: Mixed rules
sections.intro:
When the process stops at a success target or a cap, a path is terminal as soon as either rule is met. For a target of \(r\) successes, reaching the final permitted trial \(N\) means that fewer than \(r\) successes occurred in the first \(N-1\) trials. It does not mean the target remains unmet after trial \(N\).

For stopping times below the cap, use the target’s first-completion event. At the cap, combine every surviving branch, keeping completion and noncompletion separate if the question needs them. If the target is impossible before the cap, all paths still end at the cap.

blocks.title: Reach a two-success target on or before a finite cap
blocks.prompt: Independent trials succeed with probability \(\frac{1}{3}\). Stop at the second success or after three trials, and let \(T\) be the number of trials made. Find \(P(T=3)\), the probability of reaching the target, and the target-completion probability given \(T=3\).

fields.label: Completion probability given stopping at three

blocks.hint: Only SS stops at two. Completing the target at three needs exactly one success in the first two trials and a final success.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(T=2)=\frac{1}{9},\qquad P(T=3)=1-\frac{1}{9}=\frac{8}{9}.\]
  2. \[P(\text{complete at }3)=2\cdot\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\cdot\frac{2}{3}=\frac{4}{27},\]
  3. \[P(\text{complete})=\frac{1}{9}+\frac{4}{27}=\frac{7}{27},\qquad P(\text{complete}\mid T=3)=\frac{\frac{4}{27}}{\frac{8}{9}}=\frac{1}{6}.\]

blocks.title: Remove paths that would already have stopped
blocks.prompt: Independent fair trials stop at two consecutive successes or after four trials. Let \(T\) be the number of trials made. Find the probability of making four trials, the probability of completing the consecutive-success target, and the completion probability given that four trials were made.
blocks.hint: Completion paths are SS, FSS, SFSS and FFSS. Their different lengths give different probabilities. No other completion path can be terminal without an earlier SS.
blocks.solution:
1. Stopping at two has probability \(\frac{1}{4}\), and stopping at three has probability \(\frac{1}{8}\). Hence

    \[P(T=4)=1-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{8}=\frac{5}{8}.\]
  2. \[P(\text{complete})=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{16}=\frac{1}{2}.\]

  3. Only SFSS and FFSS complete at the fourth trial, with combined weight \(\frac{1}{8}\). Therefore

    \[P(\text{complete}\mid T=4)=\frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{5}{8}}=\frac{1}{5}.\]

blocks.html: Do not extend a path after its stopping rule has fired. In a consecutive-success game, a listed long string may contain an earlier terminal pattern. Include it only through that first stopping point, or count its full continuations in a way that preserves the original terminal probability.

A total-success target and a consecutive-success target need different information. For the former, track the number of successes so far. For the latter, track the recent run of successes as well. Overlapping success windows are not independent trials, so a waiting time for a pattern must not automatically be assigned a geometric parameter equal to the pattern’s single-window probability.

Check the final table and the conditioning event. The terminal probabilities must sum to one, time values must lie within the permitted range, and reward values must follow the stated rule. Divide by a conditioning probability only when it is positive; for example, some late stopping events are impossible when success is certain.

glossary.definition: The trial on which a specified numbered success first occurs.
The part of a trial sequence before the final success being fixed.
An additional waiting time beginning with new independent trials after a previous success.
A fixed maximum number of trials that ends the process even if its success target is unmet.
A complete history that ends at the first point where a stopping rule is satisfied.
Whether the success target was reached when the experiment stopped.
The total probability assigned to a final stopping-time value after all its terminal histories are combined.
A probability table formed by mapping terminal histories to their stated rewards.
A target requiring an uninterrupted run of successes rather than merely a given total count.
Counting an extended history as a new terminal path even though its process would already have stopped earlier.

examples.title: Fix the final success and count the earlier success positions
examples.question: Independent trials each succeed with probability \(\frac{1}{3}\). Find the probability that the second success occurs on trial six.
solution: Trial six must be a success. The first five trials must contain exactly one success, so the second success has not already occurred.

The earlier success can occupy any one of five positions. Each permitted complete pattern contains two successes and four failures:

\[P(\text{second success on trial }6)=\binom{5}{1}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^4=\frac{80}{729}.\]

The coefficient is \(\binom{5}{1}\), not \(\binom{6}{2}\), because the final success position is already fixed. Counting all two-success patterns in six trials would also include cases whose second success occurs earlier.
The condition “exactly one success among the first five” ensures no permitted pattern has already reached the two-success target before trial six.

examples.title: A fresh wait after success uses new independent trials
examples.question: Trials are mutually independent and each succeeds with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). Let \(X\) count trials through the first success, and let \(Y\) count additional trials after that success through the second success. Find \(P(X=2,Y=3)\) and \(P(Y>2\mid X=4)\).
solution: The first successful trial belongs to \(X\). The next trial starts the count \(Y\), so both waiting variables begin at one. The fresh independent trials have the same success probability.

The joint event \(X=2,Y=3\) is the stopped pattern FSFFS. Its two waiting segments have probabilities \(\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{2}{5}\) and \((\frac{3}{5})^2\cdot\frac{2}{5}\):

\[P(X=2,Y=3)=\left(\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{2}{5}\right)\left(\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^2\cdot\frac{2}{5}\right)=\frac{108}{3125}.\]

Knowing that the first success was on trial four fixes past outcomes. It leaves the subsequent independent trials unchanged. The condition has positive probability, so

\[P(Y>2\mid X=4)=\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^2=\frac{9}{25}.\]

More generally, a joint event \(X=a,Y=b\) consists of \(a-1\) failures, success, then \(b-1\) failures and success. Its probability factors into the two geometric waiting probabilities. This justifies independence of the separate waits under the stated independent-trial model.

examples.title: The final stopping-time value combines success and failure at the cap
examples.question: Independent trials succeed with probability \(\frac{1}{3}\). Stop at the first success or after four trials, whichever happens first. Let \(T\) be the number of trials actually made. Construct its distribution and split the final mass according to whether trial four succeeds or all four trials fail.
solution:
For stopping times one, two and three, the experiment must end in a first success:

\[P(T=1)=\frac{1}{3},\qquad P(T=2)=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{9},\]\[P(T=3)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2\cdot\frac{1}{3}=\frac{4}{27}.\]

To make four trials, only the first three must fail. Trial four is performed and the experiment then stops regardless of its result:

\[P(T=4)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^3=\frac{8}{27}.\]

\(t\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)\(4\)
\(P(T=t)\)\(\frac{1}{3}\)\(\frac{2}{9}\)\(\frac{4}{27}\)\(\frac{8}{27}\)

The probabilities total \(\frac{9+6+4+8}{27}=1\).

The two terminal histories at time four are FFFS and FFFF:

\[P(\mathrm{FFFS})=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^3\cdot\frac{1}{3}=\frac{8}{81},\]\[P(\mathrm{FFFF})=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^4=\frac{16}{81}.\]

Their sum is \(\frac{24}{81}=\frac{8}{27}\), the final stopping-time mass. Using only \(\frac{8}{81}\) for \(T=4\) would omit unsuccessful runs that reach the cap.

examples.title: Calculate capped-wait moments from its full finite table
examples.question: Use the stopping time from Worked example 3: success probability \(\frac{1}{3}\), stopping at the first success or the four-trial cap. Find \(E(T)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\).
solution:
The complete table is

\(t\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)\(4\)
\(P(T=t)\)\(\frac{9}{27}\)\(\frac{6}{27}\)\(\frac{4}{27}\)\(\frac{8}{27}\)

Weight the actual stopping times:

\[E(T)=1\cdot\frac{9}{27}+2\cdot\frac{6}{27}+3\cdot\frac{4}{27}+4\cdot\frac{8}{27}=\frac{65}{27}.\]

Use the same full table for the second moment:

\[E(T^2)=1^2\cdot\frac{9}{27}+2^2\cdot\frac{6}{27}+3^2\cdot\frac{4}{27}+4^2\cdot\frac{8}{27}=\frac{197}{27}.\]

\[\operatorname{Var}(T)=\frac{197}{27}-\left(\frac{65}{27}\right)^2=\frac{1094}{729}.\]

The uncapped first-success mean would be three. The capped variable is different: it can never exceed four, and its correct mean comes from the capped table.

examples.title: A reward may distinguish histories with the same stopping time
examples.question: A fair coin is tossed independently until the first head or until three tosses have been made. The gross reward \(R\), measured in pounds, is £4 if the first head is on toss one or two, £1 if it is on toss three, and £0 if no head appears. Construct the reward distribution, calculate its mean and variance, and find the probability of a £1 reward given that three tosses were made.
solution: The terminal paths H, TH, TTH and TTT have probabilities \(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{8},\frac{1}{8}\), respectively. H and TH both give reward four; TTH gives one; TTT gives zero.

\(r\)\(0\)\(1\)\(4\)
\(P(R=r)\)\(\frac{1}{8}\)\(\frac{1}{8}\)\(\frac{3}{4}\)

Stopping after three tosses combines TTH and TTT, but their rewards differ. A stopping-time table alone does not identify the reward unless the reward rule is also tracked.

\[E(R)=0\cdot\frac{1}{8}+1\cdot\frac{1}{8}+4\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{25}{8},\]\[E(R^2)=0^2\cdot\frac{1}{8}+1^2\cdot\frac{1}{8}+4^2\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{97}{8},\]\[\operatorname{Var}(R)=\frac{97}{8}-\left(\frac{25}{8}\right)^2=\frac{151}{64}.\]

The mean is in pounds and the variance in squared pounds.

Let \(T\) be the number of tosses made. The event \(T=3\) has probability \(\frac{1}{4}\), and the joint event \(R=1,T=3\) has probability \(\frac{1}{8}\). Hence

\[P(R=1\mid T=3)=\frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{1}{2}.\]

examples.title: Stop at a success-count target or the cap
examples.question: Independent trials have success probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). Stop when the second success occurs or when four trials have been made. Let \(T\) be the stopping time. Construct its distribution, find the probability of reaching the two-success target, and find that probability conditional on \(T=4\).
solution:
Stopping at two requires SS. Stopping at three requires SFS or FSS:

\[P(T=2)=\frac{1}{4},\qquad P(T=3)=2\cdot\frac{1}{8}=\frac{1}{4}.\]

Reaching trial four means that the first three trials have fewer than two successes. Their permitted counts are zero and one:

\[P(T=4)=\frac{\binom{3}{0}+\binom{3}{1}}{8}=\frac{1}{2}.\]
\(t\)\(2\)\(3\)\(4\)
\(P(T=t)\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)

To complete the target on trial four, the first three trials contain exactly one success and the fourth succeeds. The valid paths are SFFS, FSFS and FFSS:

\[P(\text{target reached on trial }4)=3\cdot\frac{1}{16}=\frac{3}{16}.\]

All other terminal paths at the cap fail to reach the target, with total probability \(\frac{5}{16}\).

Combining early and final-trial completion gives

\[P(\text{target reached})=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{16}=\frac{11}{16}.\]

Within the positive-probability condition \(T=4\),

\[P(\text{target reached}\mid T=4)=\frac{\frac{3}{16}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{3}{8}.\]

A run that reaches the cap need not have failed; some runs reach their target on the final permitted trial.

examples.title: Consecutive successes require a different state than a total success count
examples.question: Independent trials have success probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). Stop when two consecutive successes occur or when three trials have been made. Let \(T\) be the number of trials actually made. Find its distribution, the probability of completing the consecutive-success target, and the completion probability given that three trials were made.
solution: SS stops after two trials, with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Otherwise a third trial is made. The length-three terminal paths are SFS, SFF, FSS, FSF, FFS and FFF, each with probability \(\frac{1}{8}\).

\(t\)\(2\)\(3\)
\(P(T=t)\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)\(\frac{3}{4}\)

There are no length-three terminal paths SSS or SSF: both would already have stopped at the earlier SS.

Target completion occurs through the length-two path SS or the length-three path FSS:

\[P(\text{target completed})=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}=\frac{3}{8}.\]

Only FSS completes the target among the paths with \(T=3\). Therefore

\[P(\text{target completed}\mid T=3)=\frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{3}{4}}=\frac{1}{6}.\]

SFS has two successes in total but not two consecutive successes. A count-only binomial condition would include it incorrectly. The stopping rule must track the relevant recent history, not just the total number of successes.

extraPractice.title: The final trial fixes the position of the third success
extraPractice.prompt: Independent trials each succeed with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). Find the probability that the third success occurs on trial five, by trial five, and after trial five.
extraPractice.hint: For the third success on trial five, the fifth trial must succeed and exactly two of the first four must succeed. For the third success by trial five, count at least three successes among the first five trials.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(\text{third success on trial five})=\binom{4}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^3\cdot\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^2=\frac{432}{3125}.\]

    The final success is fixed in position five; only the earlier success positions are chosen.

  2. Let \(Z\) count successes in the first five trials. Then \(Z\sim\mathrm{B}\left(5,\frac{2}{5}\right)\), and

    \[P(Z\ge3)=\sum_{r=3}^{5}\binom{5}{r}\cdot\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^r\cdot\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{5-r}=\frac{992}{3125}.\]
  3. \[P(\text{third success after trial five})=1-\frac{992}{3125}=\frac{2133}{3125}.\]

    Having exactly three successes among five trials does not guarantee that the third occurs on the fifth.

extraPractice.title: Independent fresh waits may have different probabilities
extraPractice.prompt: A first process uses independent trials with success probability \(\frac{1}{3}\) until its first success; let its trial count be \(X\). A separate, independent process uses success probability \(\frac{1}{2}\) until its first success; let its count be \(Y\). Find \(P(X=1,Y=3)\), \(P(X+Y=4)\), and the probability that both processes finish within their own first two trials.

fields.label: Both processes finish within two trials

extraPractice.hint: The processes are independent, but their success probabilities differ. For a total wait of four, use the disjoint positive-integer pairs \((1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(X=1,Y=3)=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3=\frac{1}{24}.\]
  2. \[P(X+Y=4)=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{8}+\frac{2}{9}\cdot\frac{1}{4}+\frac{4}{27}\cdot\frac{1}{2}=\frac{37}{216}.\]

    Each term uses the correct first-success probability for each separate process.

  3. \[P(X\le2,Y\le2)=\left[1-\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2\right]\cdot\left[1-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2\right]=\frac{5}{9}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=\frac{5}{12}.\]

    The total waiting time starts at two, so it is not itself a first-success geometric variable.

extraPractice.title: The cap value includes either result on the final trial
extraPractice.prompt: Independent trials succeed with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). Stop at the first success or after three trials, whichever occurs first. Let \(T\) be the number of trials actually made. Find \(P(T=3)\), the probability of finding a success by the time the process stops, \(E(T)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\).

fields.label: Probability of success by the stopping time

extraPractice.hint: The third trial is made whenever the first two failed. It is made whether its result is a success or a failure. Build the complete three-value trial-count table before taking its moments.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(T=1)=\frac{2}{5},\qquad P(T=2)=\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{2}{5}=\frac{6}{25},\qquad P(T=3)=\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^2=\frac{9}{25}.\]

    The probabilities sum to one. The last entry does not need a success factor.

  2. \[P(\text{success by stopping})=1-\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^3=\frac{98}{125}.\]
  3. \[E(T)=1\cdot\frac{2}{5}+2\cdot\frac{6}{25}+3\cdot\frac{9}{25}=\frac{49}{25}.\]
  4. \[E(T^2)=1\cdot\frac{2}{5}+4\cdot\frac{6}{25}+9\cdot\frac{9}{25}=\frac{23}{5},\]\[\operatorname{Var}(T)=\frac{23}{5}-\left(\frac{49}{25}\right)^2=\frac{474}{625}.\]

    This variance comes directly from the finite stopping table; no infinite waiting-time variance formula is needed.

extraPractice.title: Equal rewards merge paths, but terminal failure stays separate
extraPractice.prompt: A fair coin is tossed until its first head or until three tosses have been made. A first head on toss one pays \(\text{£}8\); a first head on toss two or three pays \(\text{£}5\); no head by the end pays nothing. Let \(R\) be the reward and \(T\) the number of tosses. Find \(P(R=\text{£}5)\), \(P(T=3\mid R=\text{£}5)\) and the exact expected reward.

fields.label: Three tosses given a five-pound reward

extraPractice.hint: The terminal paths are H, TH, TTH and TTT, with probabilities \(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{8},\frac{1}{8}\). The two paths with three tosses pay different rewards.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The five-pound reward combines TH and TTH:

    \[P(R=\text{£}5)=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}=\frac{3}{8}.\]

  2. Only TTH both pays five pounds and uses three tosses. Therefore

    \[P(T=3\mid R=\text{£}5)=\frac{1}{8}\div\frac{3}{8}=\frac{1}{3}.\]

  3. The reward table has values zero, five and eight pounds with respective probabilities \(\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{8},\frac{1}{2}\). Thus

    \[E(R)=0\cdot\frac{1}{8}+5\cdot\frac{3}{8}+8\cdot\frac{1}{2}=\frac{47}{8}\ \text{pounds}.\]

    Merging TTH and TTT by their common toss count would lose the information required for the reward distribution.

extraPractice.title: A finite cap still defines a trial count when success is impossible
extraPractice.prompt: A process makes independent trials with success probability \(p\), stopping at its first success or after five trials. Let \(T\) be the number made. If \(p=0\), find \(E(T)\) and the probability of finding a success. If \(p=1\), find \(E(T)\), and decide whether the probability of success given \(T=5\) is defined.

fields.label: Success probability when success is impossible
Conditional probability given five trials when success is certain

options.undefined: Undefined: the condition has probability zero

extraPractice.hint: Use the stopping rule directly at the endpoints. A capped trial count remains finite when no success can occur. A conditional probability still requires a positive-probability conditioning event.
extraPractice.solution:
1. If \(p=0\), all five trials fail and the cap stops the process. Hence \(T=5\) with probability one, \(E(T)=5\), and success probability is zero. No finite uncapped first-success variable is being assumed.

  2. If \(p=1\), the first trial succeeds and the process stops immediately, so \(T=1\) with probability one and \(E(T)=1\).

  3. In that second case \(P(T=5)=0\). A probability conditioned on \(T=5\) is therefore undefined, rather than zero or one.

extraPractice.title: Fix the last success
extraPractice.prompt: Each independent trial succeeds with probability \(\frac12\). Find the probability the second success occurs at trial five.
extraPractice.hint: There must be one success among the first four trials and a success at trial five.
extraPractice.solution:
There must be one success among the first four trials and a success at trial five.

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{8}\)

extraPractice.title: Keep the two waiting times separate
extraPractice.prompt: Two independent sequences both succeed with probability \(\frac12\) per trial. Find the probability their first successes both occur at trial two.
extraPractice.hint: Each sequence must fail and then succeed. Multiply the two sequence probabilities.
extraPractice.solution:
Each sequence must fail and then succeed. Multiply the two sequence probabilities.

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{16}\)

extraPractice.title: Find a marked position
extraPractice.prompt: Shuffle four white counters and one red counter. Find the probability the red counter first appears on draw three.
extraPractice.hint: Each of the five positions is equally likely for the unique red counter.
extraPractice.solution:
Each of the five positions is equally likely for the unique red counter.

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{5}\)

extraPractice.title: Stop on either event
extraPractice.prompt: Independent trials succeed with probability \(\frac35\). Stop after two successes or after the first failure. Find the probability the stopping time is exactly two.
extraPractice.hint: The first trial must succeed. Either outcome of the second trial stops the experiment.
extraPractice.solution:
The first trial must succeed. Either outcome of the second trial stops the experiment.

  • Answer: \(\frac{3}{5}\)

starters.title: Stop at the second success or at the fourth trial
starters.question: Independent trials each succeed with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). Stop as soon as two successes have occurred or after four trials, whichever happens first. Let \(T\) be the number of trials made. Find \(P(T=4)\), the probability of reaching two successes before or on the final permitted trial, \(E(T)\), \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\), and the probability of reaching two successes given that \(T=4\).
starters.hint: The process cannot stop before trial two. It reaches trial four precisely when the first three trials contain at most one success. Among the paths reaching four, distinguish those that obtain the second success there from those that stop only because of the cap.
starters.solution:
1. \[P(T=2)=\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^2=\frac{4}{25},\qquad P(T=3)=2\cdot\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^2\cdot\frac{3}{5}=\frac{24}{125}.\]
  2. \[P(T=4)=\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^3+\binom{3}{1}\cdot\frac{2}{5}\cdot\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^2=\frac{81}{125}.\]

    The three trial-count probabilities sum to one.

  3. Reaching the target by trial four is equivalent to at least two successes in the first four independent trials:

    \[P(\text{target reached})=\sum_{r=2}^{4}\binom{4}{r}\cdot\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^r\cdot\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{4-r}=\frac{328}{625}.\]
  4. \[E(T)=2\cdot\frac{4}{25}+3\cdot\frac{24}{125}+4\cdot\frac{81}{125}=\frac{436}{125},\]\[E(T^2)=4\cdot\frac{4}{25}+9\cdot\frac{24}{125}+16\cdot\frac{81}{125}=\frac{1592}{125}.\]\[\operatorname{Var}(T)=\frac{1592}{125}-\left(\frac{436}{125}\right)^2=\frac{8904}{15625}.\]

  5. To reach the target on trial four, the first three must contain exactly one success and the fourth must succeed:

    \[P(\text{second success on four})=\binom{3}{1}\cdot\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^2\cdot\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^2=\frac{108}{625}.\]\[P(\text{target reached}\mid T=4)=\frac{108}{625}\div\frac{81}{125}=\frac{4}{15}.\]

    The probability of making four trials is not itself the probability of completing the two-success target.

starters.title: A successful first stage opens an independent second stage
starters.question: Stage A uses success probability \(0.3\) on independent attempts. Stop stage A at its first success or after two attempts. If it fails on both attempts, end the whole process. If stage A succeeds, start a fresh independent stage B, whose success probability is \(0.5\) per attempt; stop B at its first success or after two attempts. Let \(T\) be the total number of attempts made across both stages. Completion means that both stages succeed within their permitted attempts. Find the completion probability, \(P(T=3)\), \(E(T)\), and the probability of completion given \(T=2\).
starters.hint: List the paths that trigger stage B and the path that ends before B begins. A total of two attempts can mean success at both stages on their first attempts, or complete failure at stage A.
starters.solution:
1. Stage A succeeds within two attempts with probability \(1-0.7^2=0.51\). Conditional on entering the fresh B stage, its completion probability is \(1-0.5^2=0.75\). Therefore

    \[P(\text{completion})=0.51\cdot0.75=\frac{153}{400}.\]

  2. Two total attempts arise from two A failures, or from an immediate success at A followed by an immediate B success:

    \[P(T=2)=0.7^2+0.3\cdot0.5=\frac{16}{25}.\]

  3. Three total attempts arise either from A succeeding first and B making two attempts, or from A succeeding second and B succeeding first:

    \[P(T=3)=0.3\cdot0.5+(0.7\cdot0.3)\cdot0.5=\frac{51}{200}.\]

    The first term includes both success and failure on B’s final attempt.

  4. Four attempts require A to succeed second and B to need its second attempt:

    \[P(T=4)=(0.7\cdot0.3)\cdot0.5=\frac{21}{200}.\]

    The complete count table sums to one, and

    \[E(T)=2\cdot\frac{16}{25}+3\cdot\frac{51}{200}+4\cdot\frac{21}{200}=\frac{493}{200}.\]

  5. The only completion path with two total attempts has one immediate success at each stage, with probability \(0.3\cdot0.5=\frac{3}{20}\). Thus

    \[P(\text{completion}\mid T=2)=\frac{3}{20}\div\frac{16}{25}=\frac{15}{64}.\]

    The first-stage failures do not create a B stage. Applying one geometric model to all attempts would ignore both the branch rule and the changed success probability.

revision.body:
Write the stopping rule before assigning probabilities. A final trial count can include both successful completion and failure at the cap.

Fix the final required success

For independent trials with constant success probability \(0<p<1\), put \(q=1-p\). The \(r\)th success occurs on trial \(k\) only if exactly \(r-1\) of the first \(k-1\) trials succeed and the last trial succeeds. For positive integers \(k\ge r\),

\[P(T_r=k)=\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^r q^{k-r}.\]

Completion by a deadline means at least \(r\) successes in that many trials. Completion on the deadline fixes its final success position.

Fresh waits and changed stages

For independent fresh waits, multiply the probabilities of a specified pair of waits. For a total wait, add all permitted positive-integer pairs; each pair is a disjoint case. Keep each stage’s success probability and its own trial numbering. If entry to a stage depends on earlier success, include that branch probability. If the success chance or dependence changes, reassess the model instead of applying memorylessness across that change.

A first-success cap collects the remaining mass

Stop at the first success or at a positive-integer cap \(N\). For \(0<p<1\), the actual trial count \(T\) has

\[P(T=t)=q^{t-1}p\ (1\le t<N),\qquad P(T=N)=q^{N-1}.\]

The last row splits into final success, \(q^{N-1}p\), and no success, \(q^N\). Keep these separate if they pay different rewards. At \(p=0\), \(T=N\); at \(p=1\), \(T=1\). These endpoint statements use the rule directly.

Build the full terminal table before taking moments

Remove paths that would already have stopped. Track completion separately from trial count, and combine paths only when they produce the same recorded value. For a finite variable \(Z\),

\[E(Z)=\sum_z zP(Z=z),\qquad E(Z^2)=\sum_z z^2P(Z=z).\]\[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=E(Z^2)-[E(Z)]^2.\]

Check that the full table sums to one. For a conditional question, retain only the conditioning event and divide by its positive probability. Reaching the cap does not itself prove completion.
